title: Synthetic Authority: Ghost Influencers, Deepfakes, and the Structural Limits of Disclosure-Based Financial Regulation
affiliations: and

detail.title: Synthetic Authority: Ghost Influencers, Deepfakes, and the Structural Limits of Disclosure-Based Financial Regulation
detail.abstract:
This Article examines the intersection of financial literacy, artificial intelligence, and financial regulation in an era increasingly defined by synthetic authority—the perception of credibility generated by algorithmic systems, artificial identities, and digitally constructed personas. While existing scholarship has focused on financial influencers and the application of antifraud frameworks, this Article argues that emerging technologies—including AI-generated ghost influencers, deepfake impersonations, and synthetic financial advisors—reveal a structural limitation in disclosure-based regulation that cannot be remedied by enhanced disclosure alone.

Modern securities regulation rests on three interlocking assumptions: identifiable speakers, traceable incentives, and enforceable liability. Synthetic actors disrupt each assumption simultaneously. Drawing from securities law, Federal Trade Commission doctrine, behavioral economics, and financial literacy scholarship, this Article reframes the issue as a regulatory design failure rather than an educational deficit. It argues that financial regulation must shift from correcting informational asymmetry—the Akerlof-derived premise underlying disclosure doctrine—to addressing identity asymmetry—the inability of market participants to verify the authenticity of the source of financial authority. The Article proposes a synthetic-aware regulatory framework organized around identity verification, platform liability, and international coordination.

title: Quantum Computing and Privacy
affiliations: Notre Dame Law School

detail.title: Quantum Computing and Privacy
detail.abstract:
Quantum computing is often described as the next technological revolution, but its most profound legal consequences do not lie in automation or the creation of sentient machines. Instead, quantum computing threatens something far more foundational to modern legal systems: the temporal durability of secrecy. Contemporary privacy law rests on an implicit infrastructural assumption that cryptographic protections provide stable and durable boundaries around personal information. Encryption makes confidentiality practicable, anonymization plausible, and data security enforceable. Quantum computing destabilizes these assumptions.

This Article argues that quantum computing introduces a structural shift in privacy law by collapsing the technological premises on which modern privacy protections depend. Advances in quantum algorithms, most notably Shor’s algorithm for integer factorization and Grover’s algorithm for accelerated search, threaten the public-key and symmetric cryptographic systems that secure digital communications, financial transactions, medical records, and government databases. As a result, vast quantities of encrypted data collected today may become readable in the future once sufficiently powerful quantum systems emerge. This phenomenon—commonly described in technical literature as “harvest now, decrypt later”—creates what this Article conceptualizes as Deferred Privacy Breach: a condition in which privacy violations are probabilistic, delayed, and potentially inevitable.

The Article develops three claims. First, it provides a foundational account of quantum computing for legal audiences, explaining how quantum mechanics enables new computational architectures that differ qualitatively from classical computing and why these differences matter for encryption and information security. Second, it demonstrates that core doctrines of confidentiality, anonymization, and reasonableness depend on the continued feasibility of cryptographic protection and therefore become unstable in a post-quantum environment. Third, it argues that existing legal frameworks are not designed to address temporally extended privacy risk. Current statutes, regulatory standards, and liability rules evaluate security at the moment of data collection or breach, not across the lifespan of information. Quantum computing therefore exposes a mismatch between technological reality and legal doctrine, revealing that privacy law has long relied on an unstated premise of computational permanence.

Rather than treating quantum computing as a distant or purely technical cybersecurity issue, this Article situates it as a governance problem that requires doctrinal, regulatory, and institutional adaptation. The transition to post-quantum cryptography, the management of long-term data retention, and the reassessment of what counts as reasonable protection in an era of deferred breach all demand legal responses that extend beyond existing compliance models. This Article demonstrates that quantum computing is an infrastructural challenge to privacy law that will force the legal system to rethink its foundational assumptions about secrecy, risk, and the temporal boundaries of privacy.

title: Where Synthetic Consumers Fail: Evidence from Four Frontier LLMs and a Large-Scale Ticketing Platform
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Management

detail.title: Where Synthetic Consumers Fail: Evidence from Four Frontier LLMs and a Large-Scale Ticketing Platform
detail.abstract: Can synthetic consumers predict what customers will buy and what they do after buying when a firm knows only basic profile information? We test this question with four frontier LLMs, 86,400 real API predictions, and 110,326 transactions from a rare live-event ticketing platform dataset. The answer is limited. The models recover some purchase preferences, especially after seeing a short purchase history. But they fail in three ways. First, aggregate accuracy hides large segmentlevel misses: the models perform well in the platform's native scene but poorly for a large segment outside that scene. Second, they struggle to predict whether buyers actually attend after purchase, even after examples of buyers who did and did not attend. Third, they often disagree about the same customer: in 70.5% of cases, the four models choose different top events. Local-language prompts reduce, but do not remove, these segment gaps. For marketing research, the implication is simple: synthetic consumers can help screen which preferences to test, but they should not replace observed customers when decisions depend on realized behavior or cell-level validity.

title: Beyond Discovery: Personalized Recommender Systems and Re-Entry Decision Support in Serialized Digital Content
affiliations: Korea University Business School and Korea University Business School

detail.title: Beyond Discovery: Personalized Recommender Systems and Re-Entry Decision Support in Serialized Digital Content
detail.abstract: Personalized recommender systems are widely studied as tools that shape digital-content selection, but their role in recurring re-entry decisions, whether users return to titles already started, remains underexamined. Drawing on decision support systems theory and bounded rationality, this study argues that personalized recommenders generate a larger reading lift when users continue started titles than when they discover new ones. We test this claim in a randomized field experiment on a digital comics platform with 400,000 users assigned to either a personalized or popularity-based display, with the same titles available in both conditions. Personalized display increases reading by returning users by approximately 145%, compared with 108% for new users; after accounting for differences in title entry, the gap remains approximately 24% versus 6%. The asymmetry is driven primarily by how deeply users read once they return. The findings reframe personalized recommenders as lifecycle-management tools rather than discovery filters alone.

title: Oversight Velocity in Digital Financial Systems: The Structural Gap Between Institutional Decision Speed and Oversight Adaptive Capacity

detail.title: Oversight Velocity in Digital Financial Systems: The Structural Gap Between Institutional Decision Speed and Oversight Adaptive Capacity
detail.abstract:
Oversight of institutional decisions in regulated sectors has historically operated on a cycle: periodic examination, annual reporting, event triggered investigation; that assumed institutional decision-making to be deliberate, documented, and slow enough for after-the-fact review to be analytically meaningful. 

Digital financial systems are operating on a fundamentally different temporal architecture: decisions are made in milliseconds, at volumes measured in billions of annual transactions, by automated systems that do not produce the decision records that conventional oversight assumes. 

This paper examines the structural consequence of this temporal mismatch; termed oversight velocity, as a distinct institutional accountability condition in digital financial systems. Drawing on evidence from payment system operations, mobile credit environments, and AI-enabled transaction processing in several significant digital financial economies, the paper argues that oversight velocity is generating structural accountability gaps that intensify with scale and accelerate with AI deployment. 

It concludes by examining what an oversight architecture adequate to the velocity conditions of modern digital financial systems would need to address.

title: The Reflective Institution: Translation Drift and the Preservation of Institutional Intent

detail.title: The Reflective Institution: Translation Drift and the Preservation of Institutional Intent

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher and practitioner. The author declares no conflicts of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human participants, patient data, or experimental interventions requiring formal ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Large-scale institutions rarely act directly on purpose, mission, or strategic intent itself. They act on the representations created to operationalize it: metrics, targets, funding models, governance frameworks, and increasingly digitalized systems of evaluation and control. These systems make coordination across scale possible. Yet they also create conditions in which institutional intent can gradually separate from the operational signals — the metrics, indicators, targets, and reporting systems used to monitor and preserve alignment across scale — that were originally created to protect it. 
This paper examines the structural process through which institutions gradually begin governing representations of intent rather than the realities those representations were originally created to reflect. It develops this argument through the concept of Translation Drift: the cumulative separation that emerges as institutional priorities are repeatedly translated into administratively legible forms such as metrics, dashboards, funding criteria, reporting structures, and performance indicators designed to make large-scale coordination possible. The central argument is not that institutions fail because of corruption, incompetence, or weak oversight. Rather, drift emerges when institutions can no longer coordinate directly through lived operational reality and must increasingly rely on abstracted signals, simplified indicators, and administratively manageable representations to govern at scale.
Conceptually, the paper contributes (1) Translation Drift as a mechanism of institutional separation, (2) the Operating Spine as a coordination architecture through which drift propagates, and (3) a reflexive extension of the framework toward scientific publishing and evaluation systems themselves.
As these representational systems become operationally entrenched inside governance, funding, and evaluation processes, they increasingly shape which realities remain institutionally visible and which gradually disappear from coordinated attention. Performance systems may therefore continue signalling that the institution is functioning coherently according to its own metrics, targets, and reporting structures even while operational reality gradually diverges from the purpose those systems were originally designed to preserve. The dashboards may remain green not because drift is absent, but because coherence is increasingly evaluated within the translated representation layer itself.
The paper extends this diagnostic recursively toward scientific publication and evaluation systems themselves, arguing that publication incentives, peer review structures, funding mechanisms, and disciplinary evaluation architectures increasingly shape which forms of scientific contribution become institutionally legible, sustainable, and rewardable. In doing so, the paper identifies a structural tension within modern knowledge systems: the same mechanisms required to stabilize rigor and large-scale scientific coordination may also make it more difficult for highly integrative or conceptually unconventional forms of inquiry to gain stable visibility within mainstream scientific publishing and evaluation systems. 
Building on the broader Coherence Programme, the paper develops a reflexive institutional framework centred on Translation Coherence, Meaning Infrastructure, and the creation of reflective capacities capable of recalibrating the relationship between institutional intent, governance systems, and operational reality.
Its central claim is straightforward but far-reaching: as institutions become increasingly dependent on metrics, dashboards, targets, reporting systems, and digital evaluation architectures to govern at scale, long-range institutional resilience may depend less on intensifying representational control and more on preserving the capacity to maintain coherent relation between institutional intent, lived operational reality, and the systems used to mediate between them.

title: Personalized Recommendation, Market Expansion, and Consumption Diversity: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment in Serialized Digital Content
affiliations: Korea University Business School, Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Operation & Decision Technologies and Korea University Business School

detail.title: Personalized Recommendation, Market Expansion, and Consumption Diversity: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment in Serialized Digital Content
detail.abstract: Recommendation systems have become foundational infrastructure for online platforms, shaping how consumers discover and consume services and products. Existing research has primarily examined whether personalized recommendation systems amplify demand concentration around superstars or diversify consumption toward the long tail, but most evidence comes from settings in which recommendation effects operate largely through redistribution across existing demand. This pattern reflects the underlying consumption architecture rather than recommendation systems themselves. This study introduces serialized digital content as a distinct consumption environment for recommendation systems. On serialized digital content platforms, users consume short episodic content, engage with multiple titles in parallel, and experience recurring wait times between releases. Together, these features create unrealized consumption opportunities: users remain willing to consume additional content but face search and matching frictions in identifying what to consume next. We argue that personalized recommendation systems can convert this unfulfilled desire into additional consumption by lowering search costs and improving preference matching, thereby driving market expansion and broader consumption across the content ecosystem. We test these arguments through a large-scale randomized field experiment on a leading serialized digital content platform involving 400,000 users and 612 titles over 91 days. Personalized recommendations substantially increase aggregate, paid, and first-time title consumption. While superstar titles continue to benefit, long-tail titles capture disproportionately larger gains, increasing overall consumption diversity as market concentration declines. Our findings show how personalized recommendations can operate as a positive-sum mechanism that simultaneously expands aggregate consumption and broadens its distribution across titles in serialized digital content.

title: Cloud Forensics, Digital Evidence Handling and Legal Practice: A Comprehensive Analysis
affiliations: London Metropolitan University, London Metropolitan University, University of Liverpool - Department of Computer Science, London Metropolitan University and London Metropolitan University

detail.title: Cloud Forensics, Digital Evidence Handling and Legal Practice: A Comprehensive Analysis
detail.abstract:
The legal profession's recent rapid adoption of cloud services has increased their reliance on cloud-hosted data across criminal, civil, and corporate sectors. While this adoption has led to some technical efficiencies regarding evidence readiness and monitoring, it has also raised significant privacy, data protection and admissibility concerns.
Aim: To synthesise technical and legal scholarship on the acquisition, preservation, and courtroom use of cloud-based evidence with emphasis on chain of custody, admissibility, privacy, and cross-border access.
Method: This work makes use of a PRISMA-guided systematic literature method, drawing upon publications from 2010 to 2024 (last search: 23 March 2025). This review identified initial studies using predefined search terms before screening these studies against set inclusion/exclusion criteria. Following this, this review utilised a snowball sampling method to include wider, relevant literature (including grey literature). This review presents its findings thematically; descriptive quantitative summaries support this analysis.
Key results: From 22 studies,  five distinct subject themes emerged: (i) cloud computing and service-provider characteristics, (ii) tools and technological approaches, (iii) privacy and security, (iv) legal and jurisdictional considerations, and (v) chain of custody, authenticity, and admissibility. These themes discuss a range of recurring issues that are not limited to any one theme; these issues relate to problems concerning provider dependence, jurisdictional ambiguity and cross-border delays, multi-tenancy, and inconsistent treatment of privacy/data protection in evidential workflows.
Contribution: This review consolidates previously fragmented findings across computing and law; in doing so, this review identifies the ongoing misalignment between provider-mediated forensic practices and regional legal obligations.
Implications: Cloud service providers and the legal institutions that use such services should establish revised interoperable technical-legal standards. In greater detail, providers should clarify their obligations and revise their documentation practices to comply with these. The results of this review also support the establishment of new empirical evaluation standards for cross-border access models and admissibility-oriented workflows.

title:
Customer Segmentation Analytics in Retail: An
Empirical K-Means Clustering Study
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title:
Customer Segmentation Analytics in Retail: An
Empirical K-Means Clustering Study
detail.abstract:
Many retail firms collect substantial transaction data but lack the organizational routines to turn that data into marketing decisions. This paper examines whether K-means clustering applied to Recency-Frequency-Monetary (RFM) features can produce commercially actionable customer segments in a retail context, and develops a theoretical account of why building this capability matters strategically. Using the publicly available Online Retail II dataset (136,571 transactions;
3,800 customers), we construct RFM features, run K-means clustering, select K = 4 through elbow
analysis and silhouette scoring, and validate the solution against K-medoids (PAM), Ward
hierarchical clustering, and a 20-seed stability test. The resulting segments — Loyal Premium
(15.2% of customers, 65.5% of revenue), Price-Sensitive (48.8%), Occasional Buyers (22.6%),
and Dormant/At-Risk (13.4%) — are well-separated (silhouette = 0.4767; mean ARI across
random seeds = 0.997) and differ significantly across all three RFM dimensions (ANOVA F-
statistics: Recency F = 4131.57, Frequency F = 3964.61, Monetary F = 14086.69; all p < 0.001; η²
ranging from 0.7581 to 0.9176). Grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory and the Resource-
Based View, this study argues that the organizational routine of conducting systematic customer
segmentation analysis — not the clustering algorithm itself — constitutes a sensing capability that
enables more adaptive, resource-efficient marketing decisions. The paper’s contribution lies in
integrating this theoretical framing with a fully reproducible empirical workflow, providing a
foundation other retail researchers can build on.

title: Quantum Computing and Artificial Intelligence Security

detail.title: Quantum Computing and Artificial Intelligence Security

detail.abstract:
Background: The maturation of post-quantum cryptography and the rapid deployment of agentic and generative artificial intelligence are converging into a single, under-examined risk surface. The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised its first three post-quantum cryptographic standards in August 2024 and selected a further algorithm for standardisation in March 2025, yet the security discourse continues to treat quantum cryptanalysis and AI system security as separate domains.

Purpose: This paper consolidates the quantum dimension of AI security into a coherent analytical frame. It examines three intersecting threat vectors, namely the cryptographic exposure of AI assets to harvest-now-decrypt-later strategies, the prospective acceleration of adversarial machine learning by quantum optimisation, and the bidirectional synergy through which each technology amplifies the offensive potential of the other, and it proposes a migration governance agenda suited to practitioners operating multi-jurisdictional AI estates.

Approach: The study adopts a conceptual and integrative review methodology, synthesising primary standards documentation, national authority guidance, and emerging peer-reviewed and preprint literature. It maps identified threats against established control frameworks, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, and the cryptographic provisions of allied national guidance, and develops a tiered migration model calibrated to data longevity and asset criticality.

Findings: AI estates present a distinctive and elevated harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure because model weights, proprietary training corpora, and inference traffic carry long confidentiality lifespans that frequently exceed plausible timelines for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. Cryptographic agility, rather than any single algorithm choice, emerges as the decisive architectural property. The convergence of quantum acceleration and adversarial machine learning is currently theoretical but warrants anticipatory governance, given the asymmetry between preparation costs and tail risk.

Implications: Organisations should treat post-quantum migration as an AI governance obligation rather than a narrow cryptographic upgrade, embedding cryptographic inventory, agility, and data-longevity triage within existing AI management systems. For the Gulf Cooperation Council region, where sovereign data initiatives and AI adoption are advancing in parallel, early alignment with internationally recognised post-quantum standards offers both a risk-reduction and a strategic-positioning advantage.

title: A Holistic Framework for Information Security Management in Financial Institutions: Policies, Risk Assessment, and Business Continuity
affiliations: Jahangirnagar University

detail.title: A Holistic Framework for Information Security Management in Financial Institutions: Policies, Risk Assessment, and Business Continuity
detail.abstract: Despite the availability of international standards such as ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and NIST SP 800-37, financial institutions frequently struggle to operationalise these frameworks into a cohesive, measurable governance architecture that satisfies concurrent regulatory obligations spanning cybersecurity, data privacy, and operational resilience. Existing research addresses individual policy domains in isolation, and no prior work has proposed a unified, quantitatively grounded ISMS blueprint that integrates multi-domain policy governance with a calibrated risk measurement model and BIA-driven recovery objectives aligned to financial-sector regulatory requirements. This paper presents a holistic ISMS framework designed as a replicable artefact through qualitative document analysis of seven operational security policies from a regulated financial institution. Three research questions are addressed: (RQ1) how six security policy domains can be synthesised into a standards-aligned governance architecture; (RQ2) how a multiplicative Risk Impact Rating (RIR) model can be calibrated to produce regulatorycompatible risk appetite, tolerance, and Management Action Trigger (MAT) thresholds; and (RQ3) what BIA-driven recovery objectives (RPO, RTO, MTPD) are appropriate for three ICT asset criticality tiers. The resulting framework is validated against ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control domains and NIST SP 800-53 control families, and evaluated via structured conformance mapping. Specific contributions include: a six-domain policy taxonomy; the RIR formula RIR = Av × (Tv + Vv) × L with empirically calibrated thresholds (≤35 appetite, 36-95 tolerance, ≥96 MAT); BIA recovery objective matrices; and a Key Risk Indicator (KRI) catalogue with RAG status thresholds. Practical implementation challenges and future directions for automated continuous monitoring are discussed.

title: Control Physiology: An Agent-Based Model of FAIR-CAM Dynamics
affiliations: and Enterprise Risk Quantification Institute

detail.title: Control Physiology: An Agent-Based Model of FAIR-CAM Dynamics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Jack Jones is the creator of the FAIR and FAIR-CAM frameworks and a co-founder of the FAIR Institute. Laura Voicu declares no competing financial interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Security risk analysis typically treats control effectiveness as a static input, yet controls degrade through configuration drift, depend on monitoring systems that may themselves be degraded, and compete for finite remediation budgets. The FAIR Controls Analytics Model (FAIR-CAM) provides the theoretical framework for these dynamics, decomposing controls into three interacting domains (Loss Event Controls, Variance Management Controls, and Decision Support Controls) but has so far remained theoretical.

We present the first agent-based model to operationalize the core FAIR-CAM dynamics, making control physiology computationally observable, and are releasing the implementation as open source. The simulation implements eight agent types, a multiplicative defense-in-depth susceptibility formula, a three-source variance model, budget-constrained remediation, and a narrative causation engine that produces a complete causal trace for every loss event. In a hospital ransomware scenario (N = 1,000 iterations), three organizational dynamics emerge that static analysis cannot represent. First, emergent operational efficacy diverges from the analytical FAIR-CAM formula by approximately 17%, driven by correlated extrinsic variance; the divergence grows linearly with extrinsic frequency and vanishes under purely intrinsic drift. Second, a sharp queueing regime transition in the remediation pipeline approximately 2.8×expected loss when budget falls below a scenario-specific threshold (5–10 engineer-hours/month in this parameterization). Third, cascading monitoring failures propagate through the VMC topology: a single degraded VMC silently compounds undetected variance across the controls it manages. These dynamics (analytic divergence under correlated variance, budget-driven regime transitions, and silent monitoring cascades) are structural properties of the FAIR-CAM architecture and should generalize beyond the specific scenario studied.

title: From Parameters to Subspaces: The Geometry of Complexity in Asset Pricing
affiliations: CUNY Baruch College, Baruch College, City University of New York, Baruch College, City University of New York and Baruch College, City University of New York

detail.title: From Parameters to Subspaces: The Geometry of Complexity in Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: Recent debates in empirical asset pricing ask whether the performance gains of highdimensional machine learning models reflect genuine economic structure or statistical illusion. We argue that this question is fundamentally geometric. Across a broad class of conditional factor models, nonlinear exposure maps and high-dimensional feature expansions ultimately generate low-dimensional return-producing subspaces. The economically relevant object is therefore not the raw parameter vector, but a point, or trajectory, on a Grassmann manifold. This perspective separates parameter complexity from structural complexity: additional parameters are useful only when they expand a stable and identifiable return signal subspace. We develop Grassmannian diagnostics for subspace stability, intrinsic dimension, curvature, effective rank, and spectral separation, and use them to distinguish adaptive complexity from diffuse overparameterization. In synthetic experiments and historical RFF-IPCA backtests, these diagnostics identify frozen configurations, locate empirical signal boundaries, and explain why the best performing models lie in a Goldilocks region of stable but nontrivial subspace motion. The results provide a geometric framework for evaluating the virtue of complexity in asset pricing.

title: A Financial System Digital Twin for Cross-Market Stress Propagation: Real-Time Network Simulation Using Graph Attention Networks
affiliations: , Texas Tech University and Independent

detail.title: A Financial System Digital Twin for Cross-Market Stress Propagation: Real-Time Network Simulation Using Graph Attention Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests. No financial relationships with organizations that could influence this study. All data used is publicly available.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes and demonstrates a financial system digital twin — a continuously-updating directed network simulation that replicates cross-market stress propagation dynamics in real time. Existing approaches to systemic risk monitoring rely on static or periodically retrained models that cannot capture the velocity of contagion during acute market dislocations. The framework presented here formally defines four properties that distinguish a digital twin from a conventional simulation — state synchronisation, bidirectionality, counterfactual tractability, and crisis fidelity — and demonstrates each property through an empirical implementation spanning 17 global equity indices across 2000–2024. The implementation combines daily DCC-GARCH(1,1) correlation estimation with rolling Granger causality tests to construct directed market networks, then trains a two-layer Graph Attention Network to classify market-days as stressed or non-stressed. Against the Diebold-Yilmaz (2012) connectedness baseline, the framework achieves AUROC of 0.972 versus 0.617, and F1 of 0.575 versus 0.045. Backtests across three crisis episodes — the Global Financial Crisis (2008), the European Debt Crisis (2011), and the COVID-19 shock (2020) — demonstrate the twin's ability to detect stress propagation ahead of conventional monitoring benchmarks. An ablation study confirms that directed network topology carries information beyond bilateral correlation alone, with shuffled-edge variants producing negligible performance degradation under random edge assignment (F1: 0.570, AUROC: 0.975), validating the network construction methodology. The framework is designed to operate on publicly available data without proprietary infrastructure, making it applicable to macroprudential monitoring at regulatory institutions.

title: Rolling Difference-in-Differences with Reversible Treatment Paths and Moderating Effects

detail.title: Rolling Difference-in-Differences with Reversible Treatment Paths and Moderating Effects
detail.abstract: This paper extends the rolling difference-indifferences framework of Lee and Wooldridge (2026) to settings with reversible treatment paths and moderating effects. The framework accommodates treatment entry, exit, and re-entry through an event-type-specific aggregation strategy, preserving dynamic patterns that may be obscured by standard staggered-adoption event studies. Exit and re-entry are interpreted as post-entry event types rather than separate assignments. The paper further shows how centered treatment-by-covariate interactions can be used to explicitly measure treatment-effect heterogeneity along predetermined baseline covariates within regression adjustment and two-stage IPWRA estimators. The empirical application revisits chain-pharmacy entry and exit in rural areas, where treatment status changes repeatedly over time. The estimates indicate persistent effects of chain entry after exit, a pattern consistent with the static-game analysis in Kim (2023), and reveal heterogeneity across baseline covariate groups. Overall, the framework provides a flexible approach for estimating dynamic and heterogeneous treatment effects when treatment status changes multiple times over time.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Models for Customer Churn Prediction in the Telecommunications Industry: A Business Analytics Perspective

detail.title: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Models for Customer Churn Prediction in the Telecommunications Industry: A Business Analytics Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial or personal relationships that could influence the study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Conducted as independent academic research at California State University, Fullerton.

detail.abstract: Customer churn prediction is a critical challenge for telecommunications companies, where retaining existing customers is significantly more cost-effective than acquiring new ones. This study presents a comparative analysis of three machine learning models-Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost-for predicting customer churn using the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset comprising 7,043 customer records and 20 features. Each model was evaluated across five performance metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and ROC-AUC. Results demonstrate that Logistic Regression achieved the highest predictive performance with an accuracy of 79.91and ROC-AUC of 0.8403, outperforming the more complex ensemble methods Random Forest (ROC-AUC: 0.8225) and XGBoost (ROC-AUC: 0.8185). These findings suggest that model interpretability and simplicity may offer advantages over complexity in structured business datasets, with significant implications for enterprise churn management strategies. This study contributes to the growing body of research on applied machine learning in business analytics by providing empirical evidence for model selection in customer retention contexts.

title: Volatility Transmission Under CBDC Uncertainty: A Quantile Time-Frequency Approach Across Currencies and Innovation Sectors
affiliations: and Inner Mongolia University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Volatility Transmission Under CBDC Uncertainty: A Quantile Time-Frequency Approach Across Currencies and Innovation Sectors
detail.abstract: This study investigates the volatility spillover dynamics associated with Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) uncertainty across major currencies (Chinese Yuan-CNY, U.S. dollar-USD, EURO-EUR, Japanese Yen-JPY, and British Pound-GBP) and key innovation-driven sectors, including artificial intelligence (AI), FinTech, renewable energy, and non-renewable energy. Employing a Quantile Vector Autoregression (QVAR) framework, the analysis captures timeand frequency-dependent interconnectedness across normal and extreme market regimes, with a particular focus on the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia-Ukraine war, and Israel-Hamas conflict. The results revealed that CBDC uncertainty particularly impacts CNY, followed by USD, JPY, GBP, and EUR at median quantiles. On the sectoral side, shocks in CBDCs have enormous spillover effects on renewable energy, followed by AI, FinTech, and non-renewable energy. In addition, the USD, Euro, and JPY imperatively transmit shocks to the system, but the GBP and CNY absorb shocks at different quantiles, even during the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Likewise, during the COVID-19 era, AI, renewable, and non-renewable energy transmit volatility, but FinTech absorbs shocks at different quantiles. During the Russia-Ukraine war, overall, renewable energy absorbs shocks, but AI, FinTech, and non-renewable energy strongly transmit volatility at lower and middle quantiles. However, during the Israel-Hamas conflict, all these indices transmit volatility significantly. The study offers valuable insights for investors and traders to manage risk and hedge their portfolios more effectively.

title: Drivers of tick distributions in Latvia: a multi‑species assessment of joint and single‑species distribution models (2017–2019)
affiliations: University of Copenhagen, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Latvian Biomedical Research and Study Centre, Latvian Biomedical Research and Study Centre, Latvian Biomedical Research and Study Centre and Latvian Biomedical Research and Study Centre

detail.title: Drivers of tick distributions in Latvia: a multi‑species assessment of joint and single‑species distribution models (2017–2019)
detail.abstract: The ecological factors shaping the distribution of key tick vector species remain only partially understood. We analysed the spatial patterns of three medically important ticks, Dermacentor reticulatus, Ixodes persulcatus, and I. ricinus in Latvia, using extensive field records from a single survey combined with high-resolution environmental predictors. We pursued two complementary objectives: (i) to model and map the spatial distribution of three epidemiologically important tick species in Latvia, and (ii) to evaluate whether a joint species distribution modelling framework provides additional inferential or predictive benefit compared with single‑species models.The joint species distribution modelling analysis did not yield stable residual association estimates across fitting approaches, so subsequent inference and spatial prediction focused on single-species distribution models using Random Forest, Boosted Regression Trees, and Support Vector Machines under spatial cross-validation. Model performance differed among species, with highest predictive accuracy for I. persulcatus (mean AUC ≈ 0.93), moderate performance for I. ricinus (≈ 0.81), and lower but above-random performance for D. reticulatus (≈ 0.69).Temperature- and moisture-related predictors, including satellite-derived indicators of seasonal land surface temperature dynamics, were consistently influential. Response curves revealed strong non-linear and threshold relationships, with D. reticulatus showing relatively narrow climatic optima, I. persulcatus associated with cooler and more humid conditions, and I. ricinus exhibiting broader environmental tolerances. Final habitat suitability maps showed clear spatial differentiation: I. ricinus had the broadest area of high suitability, I. persulcatus displayed a more regionally structured pattern, and D. reticulatus was restricted to patchier areas.Our results suggest that, at the spatial scale considered, strong environmental filtering dominated species distributions, limiting the added value of joint modelling relative to more stable single‑species approaches. Together, these results provide a spatially robust and ecologically grounded distribution assessment for ticks in Latvia. The findings support public-health surveillance, identify regions of elevated potential exposure, and highlight the need to investigate additional ecological mechanisms, beyond species interactions, that shape tick communities across the Baltic region.

title: The Field of Needs  -  Subjective Prices and a Semantic Foundation for Consumer Theory

detail.title: The Field of Needs  -  Subjective Prices and a Semantic Foundation for Consumer Theory
detail.abstract: Standard consumer theory describes the syntax of choice-which orderings are consistent with observed behavior-but is, by construction, silent on its semantics: what generates the orderings, with what urgency, in which state. Ordinalism is an informational compression that preserves the rank of consistent choices while discarding the motivational substance beneath them. This paper develops a need-based foundation that restores the discarded layer. The primitive object is the marginal need field β i , a vector field assigning to each basket-state pair the marginal intensity of residual need for each good; it is not derived from a utility function but is the structure from which, under precise conditions, a utility potential may be reconstructed. From the need coefficient β i,k descends the operational object of the theory, the subjective price π i,k = p k /β i,k : at equal market prices, a good for which need is more intense is subjectively cheaper, and choice becomes arbitrage across needs until perceived costs per unit of need are aligned. The central theoretical result is that the field may, but need not, admit a global potential. When the cross-partials of β i are symmetric, the field is the gradient of a utility function and the neoclassical apparatus is recovered in full-with marginal utility reinterpreted as marginal need, and utility itself as the negative of cumulated residual need (U i =-N i). When the cross-partials are asymmetric, no global potential exists; valuations remain locally well-defined but become path-dependent, giving endowment effects, context dependence, and homeostatic consumption cycles a natural formalization rather than ad hoc corrections. Money is treated as a good with its own need coefficient β i,M (R i), decreasing in income, yielding a micro-foundation of the pain of paying and of liquidity preference. The exchange economy is reread as the alignment of subjective prices, and a hidden-Markov econometric protocol delivers testable restrictions that make the framework falsifiable on transaction data.

title: Effect of Remote Work on the Child Penalty: Evidence from the United States
affiliations: MIT and Stanford University

detail.title: Effect of Remote Work on the Child Penalty: Evidence from the United States
detail.abstract: We study the effect of the post-COVID expansion of remote work on the child penalty. Our empirical design proceeds in three steps: using pseudo-panels to estimate child penalties across occupations, exploiting cross-occupational variation in remote work adoption, and using synthetic controls to adjust for differential pre-COVID trajectories. Remote work reduces the hours penalty for mothers: each percentage point increase in an occupation's remote work share raises mothers' hours worked by 0.23%, eliminating one-sixth of the baseline motherhood penalty for the average remote occupation. We find no effects on employment, income, or wages for mothers, and no average effects on men.

title: Organic Farming, Soil Health, and Farmer Perceptions: A Dynamic Structural Econometric Model
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, , Cornell University - Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management, Cornell University, Applied Economics & Management, Cornell University and Cornell University

detail.title: Organic Farming, Soil Health, and Farmer Perceptions: A Dynamic Structural Econometric Model
detail.abstract: In some production processes, there may be an input that is advantageous in the short run but detrimental in the long run, and producers may not be fully aware of its adverse long-run effects.  One such input in the context of agricultural production are pesticides: while pesticides may have the initial effect of increasing crop yields, recent insights from soil science show that over time they exert an indirect negative effect on crop yields through their negative effects on soil health. Farmers may not be fully aware of soil microbiomes, however, and as a consequence, may not be making optimal decisions about pesticide use and organic farming adoption.  We develop and estimate a dynamic structural econometric model of farmer pesticide use decision-making to examine whether farmers are aware of and account for soil microbiomes.  Empirical results show that farmers are acting as if the clean soil stock has very little effect on crop yields, when in fact it increases yields.  We use our parameter estimates to simulate counterfactual scenarios in which farmers' beliefs about soil microbe-based ecosystem services are brought in line with findings from plant and soil sciences. We find that informing farmers about soil microbiomes decreases pesticide use, increases organic adoption, and increases farmer welfare.

title: Wind Turbines, Microclimates, and Agricultural Productivity: Parcel-Level Evidence from the U.S
affiliations: Renmin University of China - School of Agricultural Economics and Rural Development, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Rhode Island - Department of Environmental and Natural Resource Economics and National Taiwan University

detail.title: Wind Turbines, Microclimates, and Agricultural Productivity: Parcel-Level Evidence from the U.S
detail.abstract: As renewable energy deployment accelerates, wind turbines are increasingly installed on agricultural land, yet their effects on crop productivity remain poorly understood. This paper examines how wind turbine installations affect agricultural yields by combining parcel-level corn yield data for more than 2.6 million farmland parcels with detailed data on over 70,000 turbines and local weather conditions in the U.S. Corn Belt. Using a distance-based approach, we show that the effects of wind turbines on corn yields dissipate beyond 10 kilometers, indicating that turbine impacts are highly localized. We then exploit variation in both spatial proximity to turbines and the timing of turbine installation in a difference-in-differences framework that compares parcels located within 0-10 kilometers of a turbine to nearby parcels 10-20 kilometers away. We find that parcels near wind turbines experience an increase in corn yields of approximately 0.4-0.8 percent following installation. The effects are larger near higher-capacity turbines, in denser turbine clusters, and for parcels located downwind of installations. Mechanism analysis suggests that turbines reduce the incidence of extreme heat and precipitation events, with little effect on average weather conditions. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest economically meaningful gains, each megawatt-hour of wind generation (valued at $30) creates $1.46 additional agricultural revenue—approximately 4.85 percent of electricity value—highlighting an overlooked agricultural productivity spillover of wind energy infrastructure.

title: Cold or Winter? Identifying Acute Temperature-Mortality Effects
affiliations: University of Oulu, University of Oulu and Utrecht University - Julius Center for Health Sciences and Primary Care

detail.title: Cold or Winter? Identifying Acute Temperature-Mortality Effects
detail.abstract: Temperature-mortality exposure-response curves are a central input to climate damage estimation and adaptation policy. The dominant sub-annual specifications, distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) and fixed-effect panel regressions, share a common vulnerability. The annual cycles in both temperature and baseline mortality induce strong concurvity between the temperature basis and seasonal controls, and the resulting U-shaped exposure-response curve conflates acute weather effects with seasonal contrast. We resolve this by an identification strategy that constrains the temperature basis to be orthogonal to recurrent seasonal variation. The approach admits estimating an interpretable season-varying effect that is not available within the standard framework. We apply the method to Chicago mortality data and find that acute temperature effects are concentrated at extreme temperatures and are absent in spring and autumn. The cold-anomaly response is concentrated in early winter. These patterns suggest a temperature-mortality relationship that is more heterogeneous than previously characterized and raise questions about how much of the standard mortality attribution to cold reflects the seasonal mortality cycle rather than acute weather responses.

title: Institutional Amnesia and Political-Epistemological Cycles in Research on Gender and Mathematics Education: A Historical-Critical Review
affiliations: and Universidad de Los Lagos

detail.title: Institutional Amnesia and Political-Epistemological Cycles in Research on Gender and Mathematics Education: A Historical-Critical Review
detail.abstract: This article presents a historical-critical review of research on gender in mathematics education that, drawing on Tuana's (2006) taxonomy of epistemologies of ignorance, proposes political-epistemological cycles as an analytical category to explain a systematic and undertheorized pattern: periods of expansion and contraction of critical frameworks do not respond to the internal logic of research but to the surges of feminist movements and the response of the sex-gender system that contains them. Institutional amnesia is identified as a mechanism that not only prevents the critical accumulation of knowledge produced in each cycle but actively suppresses knowledge that questions the foundations of the field. The analysis spans from Fennema's foundational work (1974) to 2026, based on a historical-documentary review in Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and SciELO using the descriptor mathematics AND gender, covering 90 selected articles. The results show the predominance of operational conceptual frameworks, the hegemony of quantitatively oriented psychological methodologies, and the reproduction of an undeclared gender binary. A thematic, theoretical, and methodological gap is identified: research has measured women against male standards; it has operated without theoretical frameworks capable of articulating mathematics education and gender from a critical perspective; and it has perpetuated a quantitative hegemony that leaves unexplored the mathematical practices situated outside the classroom. These gaps are not correctable flaws: they are the result of a structural relationship between research and the systems of power that decide what mathematical knowledge matters. Recognizing that knot is the condition for beginning to undo it.

title: Brief of Amicus Curiae Ron D. Katznelson in support of appellant, in New Vision Gaming v. SG Gaming, Federal Circuit Case: 20-1400
affiliations: Bi-Level Technologies

detail.title: Brief of Amicus Curiae Ron D. Katznelson in support of appellant, in New Vision Gaming v. SG Gaming, Federal Circuit Case: 20-1400
detail.abstract:
This case presents a precedent-setting Question of exceptional importance: Whether the structure for instituting and funding AIA trial reviews violates the Due Process Clause in view of Tumey v. Ohio, 273 U.S. 510 (1927), and its progeny, which establish “structural bias” as a violation of due process.

The focus of this Amicus brief is on the financial incentives and the performance measures of any Administrative Patent Judge (APJ) serving on the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) at the US Patent & Trademark Office (PTO). Specifically, APJs are awarded Decisional Unit (DU) credits for the work done on decisions they make in adjudicating any ex parte appeal, Inter Partes Review (IPR), Post Grant Review (PGR), or Covered Business Method Reviews (CBM), the latter three are also called AIA Trials. The larger the number of DU credits APJs receive, the easier it is for them to obtain larger bonus awards and improve their opportunity for a salary increase.

This brief is directed only to the “structural bias” as it exists with the APJs themselves—whether their pecuniary interest in obtaining more DUs constitutes bias in their decision to institute more AIA trials, thereby ensuring more work for them and thereby increasing the DUs they earn. The PTO has argued elsewhere that APJs’ DU credits are fungible—that the PTAB has a significant backlog of ex parte appeals and that APJs can work on such appeals to earn more DU credits without having to grant petitions to institute AIA trials.

This Brief shows that this PTO proposition is false and that APJs do not only have the capability and substantial incentives to earn the same number of DUs by working significantly fewer hours through institution and work on AIA trials, but that they are also subject to other organizational impediments and may be forbidden from taking on additional ex parte appeal work. As such, APJ’s are manifestly subject to “structural bias” to institute more AIA trials, in violation of the Due Process Clause.

title: Wild plants and vineyards in North-Eastern Italy: two isolated systems for 16SrV group phytoplasmas in flavescence dorée epidemiology?

detail.title: Wild plants and vineyards in North-Eastern Italy: two isolated systems for 16SrV group phytoplasmas in flavescence dorée epidemiology?
detail.abstract: Flavescence dorée is one of the most impactful diseases for European viticulture. Recently, a more complex epidemiology than previously thought has been described. Scaphoideus titanus is still considered the most important vector, and Vitis vinifera (grapevine) the primary host; however, some species, such as Alnus glutinosa, Clematis vitalba, Corylus avellana, Ailanthus altissima and Salix spp. could serve as reservoirs for some FD-associated phytoplasma strains. This study aims to determine whether wild plants could represent a potential source of inoculum for vineyards in North-Eastern Italy. Therefore, phytoplasma strains from grapevine and wild plants were collected in three different provinces of North-Eastern Italy, and characterized on map and vmpA genes. Our results demonstrated that the genotypes found in grapevine (M54 and M3) were typical of the geographical area, and that wild plants contained genotypes associated with FD outbreaks and transmissible by S. titanus in other European regions, with the exception of the M3 genotype, reported for the first time in wild plants in North-Eastern Italy. For instance, C. vitalba contained, independently of the sampling area, strains ascribable to the M51 genotype, epidemic in Serbia; similarly, A. glutinosa showed the M50 genotype, typical of FD outbreak in several European areas. Analysis of the vmpA gene confirmed that phytoplasma strains belonging to Vectotype II colonize only grapevine in the areas of study, while few grapevines and all wild plants contained strains of Vectotype III. Overall, our results demonstrated that infections of grapevine and wild plants appear to be two rather distinct and isolated systems.

title: Net Energy Surplus, Complexity Maintenance, and the Limits of Economic Sustainability
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Net Energy Surplus, Complexity Maintenance, and the Limits of Economic Sustainability
detail.abstract: Long economic waves characterised by recurrent inflationary regimes, real-wage compression, rising inequality, and clustered systemic crises are well documented across pre-industrial and modern history, yet remain fragmented across monetary, institutional, demographic, and technological explanations. This paper advances a unifying biophysical constraint: the long-run viability of large-scale economic organisation is bounded by net energy surplus rather than by gross output, prices, or policy choice alone. Declining effective energy return on investment (EROI) is formalised as a systemic throughput constraint that compresses discretionary surplus, increases the maintenance burden of institutional and infrastructural complexity, and progressively reduces adaptive capacity. Integrating biophysical economics with complexity and stability theory, the paper argues that persistent surplus erosion drives economies toward nonlinear stress regimes in which instability emerges endogenously and crises cluster rather than dissipate. The framework accounts for recurring reorganisation of price structures around essentials, prolonged real-wage compression, expansion of financial buffering mechanisms, and increasing institutional rigidity during extended periods of systemic stress. Rather than proposing an alternative theory of economic cycles, the paper specifies a necessary feasibility condition that coherent accounts of sustainability, growth, and socio-technical transition must satisfy. The central implication is that durable economic sustainability depends not simply on technological substitution or policy optimisation, but on preserving sufficient net surplus to maintain, reproduce, and adapt complex socio-technical systems over time.

title: Frailty-Aware Transformer for Recurrent Survival Modeling of Driver Idle Duration in Ride-Hailing Platforms
affiliations: University of Toronto, University of Toronto and University of Toronto

detail.title: Frailty-Aware Transformer for Recurrent Survival Modeling of Driver Idle Duration in Ride-Hailing Platforms
detail.abstract: Ride-hailing platforms operate in high-frequency, behavior-driven environments characterized by recurrent participation decisions. This study examines an important but understudied driver behavior: when drivers leave ride-hailing platforms during idle periods. We formulate it as a recurrent survival process. While survival analysis offers a natural framework for duration modeling, standard approaches struggle to represent recurrent, history-dependent participation dynamics observed in ride-hailing systems. This study proposes two Transformer-based Cox survival models for recurrent idle-duration analysis. The first integrates a causal Transformer encoder to capture long-term temporal dependencies in sequential idle behavior. The second augments this formulation with a driver-specific frailty term to account for latent heterogeneity. Together, the models improve personalized estimation of idle duration and time-to-exit hazard by leveraging historical activity sequences. The framework is validated using ride-hailing data from the City of Toronto between January 2 and March 13, 2020. Results demonstrate that the frailty-augmented model achieves the highest discriminative performance and consistently strong calibration across selected follow-up horizons.

title: The Value of Safety: Evidence from a Survey of the General Public in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
affiliations: Department of Agricultural & Resource Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, World Bank, World Bank - Health, Nutrition and Population Global Practice and Government of the United States of America - Argonne National Laboratory

detail.title: The Value of Safety: Evidence from a Survey of the General Public in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
detail.abstract: designed and conducted a stated preference survey to elicit the general public’s willingness to pay (WTP) for mortality risk reductions in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Attention was restricted to i) transportation accident risks and ii) workplace, domestic and other accident risks. We asked respondents whether they would tolerate a specified increase in the cost of living (expressed in riyals per year) to obtain a reduction in the risk of an accident and/or in the chance of dying in it, conditional on the occurrence of the accident in the first place. We subsequently asked respondents to reveal the largest increase in the cost of living they would accept for that risk reduction. We estimate the accident VSL (i.e., the WTP per unit of risk reduction) to be between $2 million and $10 million (2024 $ at the nominal exchange rate). These figures are consistent with those that we would obtain through benefit transfers of the VSL from US government agencies or international organizations, and from extrapolating from earlier studies about similar types of accidents. The VSL for non- transportation accidents is about 42% greater than that in the transportation accident setting. The respondents were willing and able to answer questions about the entities that should be responsible for risk prevention, and offered a balanced attribution of responsibility to the government and to individuals (or firms), but their opinions about responsibility do not explain the VSL. Household income is likewise only loosely related to the WTP.

title: Changing the game: fast mover advantage in household solar and battery programs
affiliations: Western Sydney University and University of New South Wales

detail.title: Changing the game: fast mover advantage in household solar and battery programs
detail.abstract: Household solar and battery programs often include more lucrative financial subsidies in early stages to support earlier adoption of technologies. There are numerous international examples of subsidy re-designs that left a 'window of opportunity' for fast moving households to lock-in higher financial support, which raises questions about unintended equity and distributional impacts. Since there is limited knowledge of recent household battery programs, we utilise postcode-level monthly data from the Australian public register of small-scale technology certificates to understand the impacts of the Cheaper Home Batteries program on the installation of household batteries, roof-top solar, solar water heaters, and heat pumps. Differential interaction regressions estimate the impacts of the program on battery installs across postcodes and event study regressions are used to understand the spillover effects onto other technologies. Over the first 10 months of the program, there were 1,363 more battery installs in each major city postcode with high socio-economic status and a history of high solar installations. This corresponds with 5.4% more houses having a battery and an additional 57MWh of capacity installed in each of these more prosperous postcodes. We find that an announced re-design of the program has coincided with a higher rate of battery installations and larger batteries being installed. Since the program started, there has been a doubling of solar PV capacity installed in more prosperous postcodes. Rather than entrench energy inequity, household programs could be designed differently with the aim of more equitable support during the early stages of household technological adoption programs.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a critical analysis of contemporary capitalist representative democracy, highlighting the ethical limitations of an economic model rooted in Pareto efficiency. It argues that the current systemic architecture does not function to elevate human quality of life; rather, it designs existence and commodities to maintain individuals in an endless cycle of productivity and consumption-a phenomenon that increasingly extends beyond the human lifespan ("post-mortal commodification"). Proposing an alternative to historical failures, including state communism, this paper introduces a novel socioeconomic paradigm: a borderless, unified Global State where resource allocation is decoupled from purchasing power and instead anchored in global justice, algorithmic calculation, and actual human need. By examining the computational limitations of market redundancy and introducing the "Abundance Inversion" framework for AI-driven resource optimization, the paper proposes a theoretical post-scarcity architecture that serves as an existential imperative rather than a mere pragmatic alternative. Finally, the paper examines the institutional, lexical, and psychological barriers preventing such a transition and proposes strategic steps for systemic implementation through prefigurative politics and global cooperation.

title: The Carbon Footprint of Remote Workers' Travel Behavior: Evidence from Digital Phenotyping Data
affiliations: IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca, IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca, IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca and Scuola IMT Alti Studi Lucca

detail.title: The Carbon Footprint of Remote Workers' Travel Behavior: Evidence from Digital Phenotyping Data
detail.abstract: Evidence on the travel-related environmental impact of remote work is mixed and inconclusive, partly due to limitations in measuring workers’ mobility. Existing studies rely heavily on self-reported data, which increases exposure to measurement errors and response bias and risks overlooking relevant trips taken on homeworking days. This study leverages a digital phenotyping approach, estimating remote workers' average carbon footprint based on their observed travel behavior. Using smartphone GPS data, we track movement trajectories and estimate CO2 emissions for a sample of Italian workers. We find that working from home is associated with shorter distances traveled and reduces daily CO2 emissions by two-thirds. Carbon savings during typical commuting hours are not offset during non-commuting windows, when additional reductions are observed. Conversely, working from alternative remote locations provides no benefit. Emission savings are achieved especially by long-distance travelers on homeworking days, suggesting heterogeneity across workers in the outcomes observed. From a policy perspective, the proposed methodology has strong potential to support companies in calculating Scope 3 emissions (Category 7), thereby better assessing (and, if necessary, correcting) employees' carbon footprints. The method also supports an objective assessment of remote workers' actual mobility demand in a context where smart working is identified as a possible solution to shield workers from price shocks in fossil fuel markets. We find that homeworkers travel shorter distances using non-emissive modes, suggesting more sedentary behavior and highlighting the need for flexible work arrangements to be accompanied by initiatives that promote an active lifestyle, such as active-mobility incentive programs.

title: Values, arguments, and trade-offs: Deliberation and preference formation for marine biodiversity policy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Values, arguments, and trade-offs: Deliberation and preference formation for marine biodiversity policy
detail.abstract: Deliberative valuation theory suggests that preferences for complex environmental goods are shaped by individual value orientations as well as social interaction and argumentative exchange during group deliberation. Yet empirical research has rarely analysed how transcendental values and the deliberative group environment jointly relate to contextual values, such as preferences for, and support of, policies. This study investigates these relationships in the context of marine biodiversity conservation, drawing on DMV workshops across Europe.We combine qualitative discourse analysis with regression models of discrete choice experiment data. Individual transcendental values were measured using the Environmental Portrait Value Questionnaire, while deliberative context was operationalised through coded indicators of argument salience. Policy preferences were analysed as aggregated policy support and choice-specific utilities in trade-off situations. We also analysed perceived influence by peers.Results show that self-transcendent values—biospheric and altruistic—are positively associated with general policy support. In specific choice situations involving explicit cost trade-offs, egoistic value orientations become more salient. Exposure to predominantly pro-policy arguments during deliberation is associated with increased policy support across both analytical levels. By contrast, self-reported peer influence is not directly related to deliberative context indicators, but appears conditional on the interaction between individual value orientations and their divergence from group-level values.These findings suggest that transcendental value salience may vary between general evaluative orientations and concrete trade-off contexts, and that deliberation may shape preference formation without necessarily being perceived as influential. The results highlight the importance of analytical level and social context in understanding biodiversity conservation policy preferences.

title: Determinants of Double and Triple Burden Morbidity Among Under-Five Children: A Spatial National Study on Bangladeshi Children
affiliations: University of Barishal - University of Barishal, University of Barishal - University of Barishal, University of Rajshahi, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Department of Sociology, Gopalganj Science and Technology University - Gopalganj Science and Technology University, Khulna University and University of Barishal - University of Barishal

detail.title: Determinants of Double and Triple Burden Morbidity Among Under-Five Children: A Spatial National Study on Bangladeshi Children
detail.abstract: Background: Childhood morbidity remains a significant public health challenge in low and middle-income countries, particularly in South Asia. Although substantial progress has been made in improving child health outcomes, a considerable proportion of under-five children in Bangladesh continue to experience single and multiple infectious disease burdens. Understanding the determinants of these disease patterns is essential for targeted interventions. Therefore, this study aims to examine the socioeconomic and demographic factors associated with single and multiple disease burdens among under-five children in Bangladesh.Methods: Data from the 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) comprising 7,513 under-five children were analyzed. Disease status was defined as a composite measure of fever, diarrhea, and acute respiratory infection (ARI), categorized as no disease, single burden, and double & triple burden. Bivariate associations were assessed using chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression was applied to identify independent determinants of disease burden. Spatial and temporal analyses were conducted to examine geographic variation and trends over time.Results: Overall, 29.54% of children experienced a single disease burden and 3.36% experienced multiple (double & triple) disease burdens. In the adjusted multinomial logistic regression model, age and geographic division emerged as the most consistent predictors. Compared to children aged 12 months, those aged 37-48 months (AOR = 0.34; 95% CI: 0.20–0.59) and 48 months (AOR = 0.30; 95% CI: 0.16–0.57) had significantly lower odds of multiple disease burden. Geographic disparities were pronounced, with children from Chittagong, Khulna, Rajshahi, Mymensingh, and Rangpur divisions exhibiting significantly higher odds of both single and multiple disease burdens compared to Dhaka.Conclusions: Childhood disease burden in Bangladesh is primarily influenced by age and geographic disparities. Targeted, region-specific interventions and strengthening early childhood care may help reduce both single and multiple disease burdens among under-five children.
