detail.abstract: We report a 200-firm pipeline audit of ESG narrative disclosure accessibility among Japanese listed companies. While 195 firms yielded a four-model consensus score, 5 were pipeline-inaccessible despite satisfying formal disclosure requirements. These inaccessible cases-ranging from web-only TCFD pages to GRI-dispersed indexes-are consistent with a disclosure infrastructure oriented toward intermediary navigation (e.g., ESG rating agencies, CDP) rather than machine retrieval. Among the 195 scored firms, inter-model dispersion is sharply asymmetric: the Global Alignment axis (N3) produces high disagreement (𝜎 ≥ 0.6) at three to six times the rate of factual axes (Future Orientation, Verifiability). We interpret this as a narrative-level indicator of declaration-level alignment claims that satisfy intermediary-facing disclosure expectations without consistently supplying the implementation logic that reduces cross-model interpretive variance. Disclosure compliance does not imply machine accessibility, and machine accessibility does not imply narrative comparability. Regulatory consolidation (ISSB S1/S2, FSA 2023 mandate) has not yet restructured the audience incentives shaping disclosure formats. Incentive design begins after observability; this paper documents the infrastructure gap that must be closed before that condition can be assumed.

title: Evaluating PhenoCam and Sentinel-2 vegetation indices for tracking phenological transitions and carbon uptake in a post-mining plantation: a multi-year comparison
affiliations: Forest Research Institute, Forest Research Institute and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Evaluating PhenoCam and Sentinel-2 vegetation indices for tracking phenological transitions and carbon uptake in a post-mining plantation: a multi-year comparison
detail.abstract: Plant phenology monitoring has advanced through the integration of near-surface and satellite remote sensing, yet their comparative performance in restored post-mining ecosystems remains poorly characterised. This study evaluated PhenoCam-derived Green Chromatic Coordinate (GCC) and Sentinel-2 vegetation indices (EVI, NDVI, SAVI) for tracking seasonal carbon uptake dynamics in a Robinia pseudoacacia plantation on reclaimed lignite mine deposits in north-western Greece over six growing seasons (2020–2025). Using eddy covariance GPP as reference, we assessed each index as a proxy for daily GPP, their ability to reproduce carbon uptake phenology transition dates, and the advantages of the multi-ROI PhenoCam approach for separating overstory and understory signals.All indices showed moderate to strong relationships with daily GPP (R² = 0.55–0.72), with GCC from the ground ROI performing best (R² = 0.72), followed by EVI (R² = 0.70). Start and peak of season dates were reproduced with good fidelity (KGE = 0.83–0.89), but end of season estimates yielded negative correlations with GPP-based phenology, a pattern attributable to structural–physiological decoupling during autumn senescence, when photosynthetic activity declines ahead of detectable changes in canopy optical properties. Optimal threshold values varied substantially among indices (0.28–0.60), confirming no universal threshold applies across vegetation indices. The multi-ROI approach revealed strong interannual variability in understory dynamics, with start of season differences between canopy and ground ROIs ranging from 1 to 52 days, a within-ecosystem signal inaccessible to satellite observations. The limited quantitative advantage of PhenoCam over Sentinel-2 is partly attributed to favourable dual-orbit acquisition geometry and should not be generalised to regions with more constrained satellite availability. These results highlight the complementary value of near-surface and satellite monitoring in forest restoration plantations and point to the integration of physiologically sensitive indices as a priority for improving autumn phenology estimation.

title: Fiscal policy transmission through production networks with heterogeneous households
affiliations: and

detail.title: Fiscal policy transmission through production networks with heterogeneous households
detail.abstract: We study how sector-specific fiscal policy propagates in an economy with heterogeneous households and production networks. We develop a multisector New Keynesian model in which input-output linkages interact with differences in households’ marginal propensities to consume (MPCs). We show that fiscal multipliers depend on sectors’ positions in the production network, as network linkages reallocate income across households with heterogeneous consumption responses. We derive an intersectoral Keynesian cross and introduce an MPC-augmented network multiplier that jointly characterize the transmission of fiscal shocks. The interaction between heterogeneous consumption responses and production networks is non-additive: network linkages can either amplify or attenuate fiscal transmission depending on how income is redistributed across households. Fiscal policy is most effective when spending is directed toward labor-intensive, downstream sectors that employ a large share of high-MPC households. Using data from the Survey of Consumer Finances, we document substantial sectoral heterogeneity in household balance sheets and in the prevalence of hand-to-mouth households. Calibrating the model to the U.S. economy, we find sizable variation in sectoral fiscal multipliers and significant distributional effects of government spending.

title: Discourse, Legitimacy, and Coercive Micro-orders: A Two-level Model of Macro-to-Micro Political Transmission

detail.title: Discourse, Legitimacy, and Coercive Micro-orders: A Two-level Model of Macro-to-Micro Political Transmission
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical model of how macro-political discourse and practice may shape micro-level conflict resolution, with particular attention to the transmission of coercive or force-centered orientations into everyday social interactions. The core claim is not that macro politics mechanically determines micro behavior, but that repeated exposure to stability-oriented discourse and exemplary coercive practice can alter agents legitimacy beliefs, perceived sanction structures, and strategy selection at the local level. To formalize this claim, the paper constructs a two-level model in which a macro variable jointly captures discursive intensity and enforcement visibility, while micro agents choose between cooperative and coercive strategies in repeated interactions. The model shows how macro discourse can shift payoff ordering, generate threshold effects, and produce a self-reinforcing coercive equilibrium when bottom-up accountability is weak. The paper contributes a mechanism-centered account that bridges discourse, incentives, and equilibrium selection. It also distinguishes this account from existing theories of discipline, habitus, and institutional incentives by specifying a formal transmission channel from macro legitimation to micro strategy choice. The model yields several testable propositions and suggests empirical designs based on survey experiments, text analysis, and interaction-level behavioral data.

title: Herding in the foreign exchange market
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) and University of Warwick

detail.title: Herding in the foreign exchange market
detail.abstract: Using a recent and comprehensive data set covering nine of the most actively traded currencies on a monthly basis from 1995 to 2024, this paper explores the presence and potential drivers of herding behaviour in foreign exchange rate forecasts. The dataset features an average of 40–50 forecasters per currency, representing a broader range of currencies, a longer time frame, and a larger cross section of forecasters than is commonly found in the FX herding literature. Our results provide mixed evidence on herding, where the balance tends towards anti-herding conclusions.While some revision-based tests suggest herding when current consensus forecasts are used, this evidence weakens considerably when lagged information is employed. In contrast, forecast-error based tests, Bernhardt et al. statistics, and over-reaction regressions more often point to anti-herding, particularly at longer horizons. Overall, we interpret the findings as suggesting thatdifferences among forecasters are largely attributable to heterogeneous views, noise, or idiosyncratic error rather than systematic convergence toward the consensus. When alternative explanations for expectation formation or revisions are considered, the main findings remain unchanged across a wide range of measures, including different types of uncertainty and FX predictors such as the forward premium, the real exchange rate, and the depreciation rate.

title:
Semi-Stillness: 
Short Puts, Short Calls, and the Three Types of Assets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Semi-Stillness: 
Short Puts, Short Calls, and the Three Types of Assets
detail.abstract:
Prior work in this research program established that there are only two fundamental trading strategies in spot markets-Mean Reversion and Momentum (Paper No. 1)-and that a synthetic third strategy (range-based options) provides "full stillness" (Paper No. 2). However, these frameworks are price-centric. They struggle to explain assets where yield-rent, coupons, dividends-is a significant component of total return. 

This paper makes three contributions. First, it introduces a taxonomy of assets based on whether they produce a yield stream: Commodities (no yield, price-only returns), Growth Assets (no yield, price-only returns, value retained), and Yield Assets (produce yield, price + yield returns). Second, it introduces semistillness: yield-enhanced strategies that function as short puts (long asset plus yield) or short calls (short asset plus yield, accounting for borrowing costs or the requirement to buy back). Third, it introduces double semi-stillness: combining a long yield asset with a short position in another asset, with only one positive yield (from the long asset). 

Crucially, semi-stillness does not eliminate the need for a directional view. The investor must still apply a positional argument-Mean Reversion (price is low, expect it to rise) or Momentum (price is high and breaking out, expect it to continue). The yield provides a buffer and an extra return when the directional view is correct, and a cushion when it is slightly wrong. However, if the directional view is substantially wrong, the buffer is overwhelmed. The paper formalizes the payoff structure, explains why yield assets exhibit lower volatility than pure price-driven assets, and connects the framework to the broader Political Systematical Trading research program.

title: Mortgage Lock-in: A Review of the Literature
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, UNC Kenan-Flagler Business School - Finance Area and Rice University - Jesse H. Jones Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Mortgage Lock-in: A Review of the Literature
detail.abstract: This chapter reviews the rapidly growing literature on mortgage lock-in and its effects on household mobility, labor reallocation, home sales, owner-occupied prices, and spillovers into rental and commercial markets. We then discuss two future research directions: (1) separately identifying lock-in effects from the direct effects of the existing interest rate on the mortgage, which have different implications for household behavior as market interest rates rise, and (2) assessing the general-equilibrium consequences of reduced mobility on labor markets and productivity. We close by discussing policy responses, including portability, broader assumability, and a Danish-style delivery option.

title:
From Employment Realization to Demand Generation:
The Macroeconomic Mechanisms and Policy Implications of Employment Infrastructure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
From Employment Realization to Demand Generation:
The Macroeconomic Mechanisms and Policy Implications of Employment Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
Existing macroeconomic theories generally treat employment as a derivative outcome of economic growth, industrial expansion, or labor market adjustment. Policy practice has likewise tended to address employment problems through training, subsidies, job matching, relief measures, and entrepreneurial incubation. However, against the background of the declining marginal effects of traditional infrastructure investment, the weakening capacity of capital and technology to absorb labor, the expansion of nonstandard employment, and the accelerating substitution of labor by artificial intelligence, the transmission mechanism through which growth automatically creates employment is increasingly becoming ineffective.
      This paper proposes the concept of “employment infrastructure” and, on this basis, constructs a
theoretical framework for “New Employmentist Economics.” Unlike traditional employment policies,
which focus on the ex post matching of existing jobs and remedial responses to unemployment outcomes,
employment infrastructure is concerned with the institutional conditions prior to job formation. Its
purpose is to organize latent social demand, human capabilities, and social resources into business entities
and stable employment.

title: Crypto has Fundamentals: A Seven-Factor Model for Digital Asset Returns
affiliations: and UCLA Anderson

detail.title: Crypto has Fundamentals: A Seven-Factor Model for Digital Asset Returns

Nijat Aliyev has no competing interests to declare. Neither author received compensation from any entity that could be perceived as having influenced the findings of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available market data and blockchain network data. No human subjects, patients, or participants were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Data was obtained through a commercial subscription to Coin Metrics Pro, purchased by the authors at standard rates. No entity had any role in the study design, analysis, interpretation, or decision to submit.

detail.abstract:
Cryptocurrency markets are widely perceived as speculative and disconnected from fundamentals. This perception keeps many traditional investors on the sidelines: without understanding what drives digital asset returns, they cannot decompose portfolio performance, hedge unwanted exposures, or distinguish skill from systematic risk. This paper addresses that gap.

We introduce the QuantNest-7 (Q-7) model, a seven-factor framework that extends the three established factors of Liu et al. (2022) (market, size, and momentum) with four new dimensions drawn from blockchain data and derivatives markets: on-chain quality, fundamental value, residual volatility, and perpetual futures funding sentiment.

Using 90 tokens over six years (January 2020 through May 2026), we find that five of six style factors carry statistically significant risk premia. On-chain quality, value, volatility, funding sentiment, and short-term reversal are all significant at the 1% level, while size becomes insignificant after controlling for volatility, suggesting the apparent size premium is a volatility premium in disguise. Notably, we document short-term return reversal rather than the momentum effect reported by Liu et al. (2022), indicating that past losers outperform past winners in our broader, more recent sample.

The Q-7 model exhibits essentially zero overfitting, explains 63% of per-token return variation and 85% of diversified portfolio returns out of sample. Conditioning on market sentiment reveals regime-dependent premia: reversal earns its strongest returns during fearful markets, value during optimistic ones, while quality delivers positive returns across all sentiment environments.

For practitioners, the Q-7 model provides the first comprehensive factor-based toolkit for digital assets: portfolio managers can decompose crypto returns into systematic exposures, construct factor-neutral portfolios, run performance attribution, and begin treating digital assets with the same analytical rigor applied to equities and fixed income.

title: Polarization and Unequal Destinations in Children's Paternal-Resource Exposure, 1980-2024
affiliations: Liaoning University

detail.title: Polarization and Unequal Destinations in Children's Paternal-Resource Exposure, 1980-2024
detail.abstract: Using IPUMS Census and ACS microdata from 1980-2024, this paper documents polarization and unequal destinations in U.S. children's paternal-resource exposure. Exposure to employed resident fathers with high-school-or-less or some-college education fell by 22.6 percentage points, while exposure to employed BA+ fathers rose by 18.3 points and no-resident-father exposure rose by 4.7 points. The aggregate gain in the average paternal-resource score was driven by compositional upgrading of maternal education; within race-by-maternal-education cells, exposure deteriorated on average. The central finding is that the same maternal credential mapped onto sharply different paternal-resource trajectories. Among children of white BA mothers, each percentage point decline in employed some-college father exposure was associated with a 0.60-point increase in BA+ father exposure and a 0.20-point decline in no-father exposure; among children of Black BA mothers, the corresponding figures were a 0.18-point increase and a 0.86-point increase, respectively. Some-college mothers across racial groups also experienced absolute deterioration. The patterns are robust to rank-weighted measures, alternative middle definitions, mother- versus child-weighted distributions, and post-1990 samples. Educational upgrading raised aggregate exposure, but the lost middle had unequal destinations across race-by-maternal-education groups, reinforcing rather than closing pre-existing gaps in children’s paternal-resource environments.

title: Household debt, the real economy, and financial stability: A literature review
affiliations: Bank of Finland and Bank of Finland

detail.title: Household debt, the real economy, and financial stability: A literature review

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Finland Research Discussion Paper No. 4/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Global Financial Crisis of 2007–2009 moved research on household debt and its aggregate implications to the forefront of macroeconomics. In this review, we offer a synthesis of this large body of both empirical and theoretical research, and an overview of the most important themes for future research. Empirical studies robustly find that rapid aggregate household debt growth is associated with an increased incidence of financial crises and slower future economic growth. There is a broad consensus in the literature, both empirical and theoretical, that this statistical association is mostly driven by changes in credit supply and lending standards. This is also the dominant view of the drivers of the Global Financial Crisis, in particular in the U.S. However, the narrative emerging from the literature, heavily concentrated on the U.S. experience, is not easy to generalize. The mechanisms that define how credit expansions ultimately lead to responses in aggregate economic activity depend both on cross-sectional het erogeneity in household balance sheets and on local credit market institutions. These factors shape the credit constraints that households face, creating externalities that can ultimately cause large output losses and slow recoveries when the economy is faced with unexpected shocks. Overall, there remains many open questions in quantifying the relative importance of credit demand and supply factors in explaining observed household credit booms and busts, as well as in understanding the theoretical underpinnings of such cycles.

title: Digital Economy Agreements: A Path To Digital Trade Law 4.0?
affiliations: University of Lucerne, University of Lucerne, Independent and University of Lucerne

detail.title: Digital Economy Agreements: A Path To Digital Trade Law 4.0?
detail.abstract: Digital Economic Agreements (DEAs) have come to occupy a distinct and increasingly significant role in the regulation of digital trade. Unlike the broader and more traditional scope of Preferential Trade Agreements (PTAs) that also tackle issues of trade in goods, services, and intellectual property rights, DEAs are directed specifically at establishing rule-frameworks for the digital economy. This article situates DEAs as a new type of treaties in context-both with regard to the global landscape of digital trade rulemaking and to its evolution over time. It offers a detailed analysis of the DEAs in place, providing insights into their legal architecture, common provisions and novel features. The article pays, in addition, particular attention to the DEAs' mechanisms to safeguard regulatory autonomy, which becomes all the more critical considering the broader set of issues that DEAs cover. The article then compares with and reveals the contrast between the DEA model and the ongoing negotiations towards an Agreement on Electronic Commerce under the umbrella of the World Trade Organization (WTO). In terms of analytical query, we highlight the advantages of DEAs as a flexible as well as a forward-oriented model of digital trade regulation that potentially is up to the challenge of keeping up with a technologically fluid environment and could pave the path towards digital trade law 4.0. This evaluation remains however nuanced, as the evidence is still out, as to whether DEAs have a real impact on the ground and whether they reduce, rather than exacerbate, the existing fragmentation in the regulation of the datadriven economy.

title: Rethinking the Development Strategy for Ethnic Minority Areas in Western China with Yuan Intelligence: Cultural Matrix, Digital Empowerment and Spatial

detail.title: Rethinking the Development Strategy for Ethnic Minority Areas in Western China with Yuan Intelligence: Cultural Matrix, Digital Empowerment and Spatial
detail.abstract: The digital economy is reshaping regional economic geography worldwide. Western China's ethnic minority regions are characterized by cultural diversity, ecological fragility, geopolitical sensitivity, and underdevelopment. Their digital transformation faces three structural dilemmas: technology suspension, development decoupling, and spatial imbalance. Drawing on anti-gradient development and borderopening strategies of the 1980s-1990s, this paper constructs a three-dimensional analytical framework: Cultural Matrix-Digital Empowerment-Spatial Reconstruction (CDS). It systematically reveals the internal logic by which digital technology drives the transformation of regional development models and spatial evolution through three micro-mechanisms: factor restructuring, network embedding, and institutional adjustment. Given the heterogeneity of the cultural matrix, western ethnic regions are divided into three types: southwest cultural-mountainous, northwest ecological-energy, and border security-port areas, each with differentiated empowerment paths and spatial governance strategies. The study shows that western ethnic regions must shift from traditional policy-scale-driven development to digital refined spatial governance, and build a new layout featuring technology rooted in locality, culture-enabled development, and spatially coordinated resilience. This paper not only provides theoretical support and practical solutions for the high-quality development of western ethnic regions in the new era, but also offers Chinese-style knowledge and path references for the digital transformation of global multi-ethnic settlements, ecologically sensitive areas, and border zones.

title:
Banking Sector Institutional Conversion Gap (BICG)
A Public Conceptual Working Paper on the Conversion of Banking Resources into Productive, Inclusive and Resilient Intermediation

detail.title:
Banking Sector Institutional Conversion Gap (BICG)
A Public Conceptual Working Paper on the Conversion of Banking Resources into Productive, Inclusive and Resilient Intermediation
detail.abstract: This working paper develops the Banking Sector Institutional Conversion Gap (BICG) as a public conceptual framework for analysing whether banks convert the resources they control into productive, inclusive and resilient intermediation. The argument starts from a measurement problem. Conventional indicators such as assets, deposits, liquidity, capital adequacy, profitability, account numbers and sovereign securities holdings are essential for banking analysis, but they do not prove that financial resources have been transformed into monitored credit, active usage, stable funding, useful payments or effective policy transmission. The BICG therefore shifts the focus from financial presence to institutional conversion. It reads banks as institutions that mobilise resources, screen information, price risk, allocate claims, monitor borrowers and connect households, firms and public policy to financial functions. The public version retains the conceptual contribution while protecting operational detail. It presents six blocks: banking transformation, savings and funding buffers, inclusion and access, regulation and risk coverage, monetary conversion, and fiscal or sovereign-exposure conversion. It explains why a bottleneck-sensitive view is preferable to a permissive average when banking functions are complementary. It deliberately avoids detailed formulas, calibration recipes, parameter values, proprietary threshold construction, software routines and institution-specific interpretation rules. The result is a publicationready working paper that can support academic debate and future empirical calibration without becoming a technical manual. The contribution is located at the intersection of finance-growth theory, banking intermediation, financial inclusion, prudential analysis, monetary transmission, sovereign-bank interdependence and composite-indicator methodology. The paper provides conceptual tables, an illustrative radar profile, a heatmap matrix, a histogram and a monthly historigram. These visuals are synthetic and non-confidential; they demonstrate how dispersion, imbalance and time dynamics can be communicated without ranking banks or issuing recommendations. The BICG is not a credit rating methodology, not a valuation tool and not an investment recommendation. It is a conceptual lens for identifying where banking-sector resources may become useful intermediation and where they may remain constrained by institutional frictions.

title: Economic Decoupling as a Readiness Signaling Device
affiliations: Université Paris V Rene Descartes and ESSEC Business School

detail.title: Economic Decoupling as a Readiness Signaling Device

publicationDetails.detailsText: ESSEC Business School Research Paper No. 2605
publicationDetails.journalName: ESSEC Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper presents a game-theoretic analysis of economic decoupling as a deterrence mechanism amid the renewed risk of international conflict between two economically integrated superpowers. In our model, a potential aggressor considers initiating military conflict, while the defender, anticipating this risk, can preemptively decouple to signal its readiness to resist aggression. We examine both a full-information game and a more realistic setting with incomplete information about the defender's priorities. Under full information, we identify the optimal degree of decoupling that ensures effective deterrence. With incomplete information, deterrence becomes more fragile: although a peace equilibrium remains possible within a narrower parameter range, hybrid equilibria, where conflict occurs with positive probability, also emerge. The results highlight how even minor informational imperfections can generate intrinsic geopolitical instability, emphasizing the fragility of peace under conditions of economic interdependence.

title: Mind the Gap: Disagreement and Credible Monetary Policy
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: Mind the Gap: Disagreement and Credible Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of interest rate disagreement between the Federal Reserve and financial markets on the transmission of U.S. monetary policy. First, I construct a simple real-time measure of disagreement and show that it improves short-and medium-horizon forecasts in standard macroeconomic VARs. Second, using lag-augmented local projections, I show that disagreement dampens monetary policy effectiveness, attenuating its impact on output and offering an explanation for apparent anomalies such as the "activity puzzle." Third, I demonstrate that market expectations, as reflected in tradable asset prices, outperform Fed staff forecasts, and that informationadvantage tests reveal no systematic Fed edge, challenging prevailing narratives. I show that standard New Keynesian frameworks with incomplete information contain a latent disagreement structure, which, when formalized, yields a parsimonious explanation of the documented evidence. The model generates disagreement from three distinct sources-fundamentals, policy rule, and credibility. A general state-space model identifies the importance of each and sheds light on key normative implications.

title: The Denationalisation of Healthcare
affiliations: Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA)

detail.title: The Denationalisation of Healthcare

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Researching into market based solutions to healthcare in the UK
declarations.ethicsApproval: It has been approved and published by the IEA.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that the UK's National Health Service (NHS), long shielded from serious public scrutiny by deep cultural reverence, is now facing a fundamental reassessment. A marked shift in public opinion has taken place, with Britons increasingly willing to acknowledge that the NHS performs worse than comparable European healthcare systems, a view supported by the evidence: in the last pre-COVID year, the UK recorded the second-highest rate of treatable avoidable mortality in Western Europe, and the NHS has consistently ranked poorly in international comparisons for decades. 

The paper makes the case for replacing the NHS with a Social Health Insurance (SHI) system, a market-based, competitive, and largely non-state model in which the role of government is not to run healthcare facilities but to guarantee universal access. Such systems consistently outperform the NHS on clinical outcomes, and this gap is not simply a function of higher spending. 

Drawing on international precedents, the paper demonstrates that such a transition is feasible. The Czech Republic and Slovakia undertook precisely this kind of systemic reform during the 1990s, as did eastern Germany following reunification. The Netherlands, meanwhile, replaced a de facto NHS-style system with a regulated, competitive private SHI model in the mid-2000s. While these examples are not directly transferable to the UK context, they illustrate that a transition between healthcare systems can be carried out in an orderly and non-disruptive manner.

The paper concludes with a proposed reform pathway for England, offering a detailed model for how the NHS could be progressively restructured into a European-style SHI system, preserving universal coverage while introducing the competitive dynamics that have driven superior outcomes elsewhere.

title: Differentiable Latent Indexing in LLMs: Toward Native Retrieval as a Cognitive Function
affiliations: Rice University

detail.title: Differentiable Latent Indexing in LLMs: Toward Native Retrieval as a Cognitive Function
detail.abstract:
The problem addressed in this work is the persistent separation between parametric memory, encoded within model weights, and non-parametric memory retrieved through external databases or retrieval systems in modern Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures. Although RAG-based systems have improved factual grounding in large language models (LLMs), they introduce architectural fragmentation between the retrieval and generation components, which are often optimized independently and coupled only at inference time. This separation introduces several limitations, including retrieval latency, semantic drift between retrieved evidence and model context, and restricted end-to-end gradient flow between evidence selection and downstream reasoning. Existing memory-augmented architectures partially address these issues but typically maintain retrieval as an external or weakly integrated process.
The DLI-LLM framework proposes an alternative architectural formulation in which differentiable retrieval mechanisms are integrated directly within Transformer layers through a latent key-value memory structure (Bahdanau, Cho, & Bengio, 2014). Retrieval queries are generated from hidden state representations and routed through learned attention-gating mechanisms, enabling the retrieved vectors to participate directly within the transformer's forward computation pathway.
The objective of this paper is not to claim empirical validation, but to formalize the architectural implications, theoretical properties, and comparative positioning of a retrieval-integrated transformer architecture within the broader landscape of retrieval-augmented and memory augmented transformer architectures (Lewis, et al., 2020; Khandelwal, Levy, Jurafsky, Zettlemoyer, & Lewis, 2019; Jégou, Douze, & Schmid, 2011; Qu, 2021).

detail.abstract: We provide the first large-scale empirical evidence assessing proposed reforms to corporate voting. We focus on "mirror voting," meaning pro-rata voting by indexed shareholders based on the proportion of votes cast by non-indexed shareholders. We find that if index funds had followed "mirror voting" for more than 600,000 agenda items from 2005 through 2025, the results would have flipped just 12 times, compared to thousands of flips if index funds had voted based on proxy advisor or management recommendations. We examine "mirror voting" flips and find that they tend to involve contentious votes. We also find that if index funds had abstained from voting, one in ten shareholder meetings would have been below the quorum threshold. Based on our results, we conclude that a "mirror voting" rule for index funds would have been the least disruptive of several reforms historically. We argue that this evidence should be considered in the analysis of the benefits and costs of proposed voting reforms.

title: Is Compute the New Oil? Cross-Asset Risk and the Case for a Dedicated Market

detail.title: Is Compute the New Oil? Cross-Asset Risk and the Case for a Dedicated Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author conducted this research independently, in a personal capacity, using only data accessible via standard commercial subscription (Bloomberg). The views expressed are solely those of the author and do not represent those of any affiliated institution. The research did not use any employer resources or confidential information, and the author has no financial interest in the exchanges, index providers, or instruments discussed. All errors are the author's own.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: GPU compute has become a multi-hundred-billion-dollar exposure underpinning AI, yet whether its price risk can be hedged with existing assets—and thus whether the dedicated compute-futures markets announced in 2026 are warranted—has, to our knowledge, not been tested. Using daily GPU rental-rate benchmark indices (via Bloomberg) for three generations (A100, H100, B200)—the first such cross-generation panel we are aware of—we ask whether compute is "the new oil": a hedgeable industrial commodity. We document its price dynamics—newer generations are far more jump-prone than oil or equities (though lower in overall volatility), with no volatility clustering—and a cross-generation price structure whose discounts shift over time. We then test cross-asset proxy hedging out-of-sample. GPU rental returns are weakly correlated (daily |ρ| ≲ 0.1) with NVIDIA, semiconductors, compute-infrastructure equities, and the broad market, and no minimum-variance proxy hedge delivers out-of-sample variance reduction distinguishable from zero—across the three generations, across horizons from daily to weekly (monthly and quarterly results are indicative only, given few non-overlapping blocks), and after multiple-testing, active-day (stale-filtered), and frontier-roll checks; a naïve one-for-one hedge sharply adds risk. This is a negative result on a short, stale sample: a power analysis shows the effective sample cannot resolve a true variance reduction below roughly 9%, so we report the absence of a detectable conventional hedge rather than proof of exact orthogonality. Even so, no detected hedge removes more than a small fraction of a jump-prone exposure, so the practical case for a direct instrument is little changed by that ceiling. We read the result constructively—a suggestive incomplete-market rationale for a dedicated market—while noting that the same weak correlation implies a liquidity paradox for those contracts, and we quantify the heightened exposures (not materially reducible by the proxies we test) in AI-training budgets and GPU-collateralized lending.

detail.title: Climate Policy and Brown Risk Premium on Bank Loans: Direct vs. Indirect Emissions

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Finland Research Discussion Paper No. 5/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The paper studies how climate policy affects the brown risk premium in bank lending, distinguishing between Scope 1 (direct) and Scope 2 (energy-related) emissions using loan level data on new variable-rate corporate loans from 2019–2024 matched with constructed measures of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emission intensity. Exploiting the Finnish Climate Act of 2022, which set a binding 2035 net-zero target, we show that Scope 1 emissions are priced throughout the sample, indicating pre-existing risk pricing, while Scope 2 emissions are priced mainly after the policy, suggesting an expansion of priced transition risks. We further isolate periods of acute energy market stress and find that banks temporarily deprioritize carbon risk during energy crisis months. Estimated carbon premia are economically meaningful, but we do not find strong evidence that pricing differs systematically between large and small firms.

title: Rethinking the Economics of a Space Elevator: From Conceivability to Possibility
affiliations: and

detail.title: Rethinking the Economics of a Space Elevator: From Conceivability to Possibility
detail.abstract: Why is it that, despite established and reasonable plausibility, humanity has not yet built, or started building, or even attempted building, its first space elevator? Answering this question of evolutionary significance is one of the two main objectives o f this paper. The other, of equal importance, is to propose a new framework, model, and instrument through which space elevators can be understood, evaluated, funded, and built. The paper addresses the baseline concept of the space elevator and the economi c narrative to date, identifying a number of challenges that may explain the current status quo. We identify three: the need for a dynamic multi-decade demand analysis, due consideration for the public good aspects of a space elevator, and a dissonance wit h our current financial value framework and equations of value. We further explore the latter two, revealing: 1) the key public good characteristics of a space elevator in the investment, construction, and utilisation stages, and 2) a financial value framework where space is not considered as integral to our models of value. We expand the discussion by digging deeper into three common and conventionally used project valuation models, Net Present Value, Cost Benefit Analysis, and Real Options Valuation. The discussion addresses the models' main structure and their applicability to a space elevator megaproject. Real options are identified as a unique possibility that could be used for a space elevator project design. However, while useful and relevant, they ne ed to be applied within a transformed value framework. We propose a space-adjusted real options model, based on the space value of money framework, along with a tailored instrument, Public Capitalisation Notes, as an alternative approach that could catalys e the necessary funding and eventual building, or attempt at building, humanity's first space elevator.

title: Violent Conflict and Cross-Border Lending
affiliations: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, TBS Business School, European Central Bank (ECB) and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: Violent Conflict and Cross-Border Lending

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: How do violent conflicts shape cross-border lending? Using syndicated loan data on 14,021 creditors and 97,169 firms across 179 countries, we document a dual response. Relative to domestic creditors, foreign lenders reduce overall lending by 27% (supply driven) but increase lending to military-related sectors by 24% (demand-driven). This reallocation is concentrated among lenders with military-sector expertise but limited country specialization, and flows toward politically non-aligned conflict zones. Pre conflict exposure to cross-border lenders is associated with divergent firm-level out comes: military firms expand assets, revenues, and employment, while exposed civilian firms contract. Violent conflicts thus selectively redirect, rather than uniformly sup press, cross-border credit.

title: Estimating Systematic Risk in a Sparsely-Traded Frontier Market: A Reproducible Beta Methodology and Sector-Level Evidence from the Mongolian Stock Exchange

detail.title: Estimating Systematic Risk in a Sparsely-Traded Frontier Market: A Reproducible Beta Methodology and Sector-Level Evidence from the Mongolian Stock Exchange

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses publicly available aggregate market data from the Mongolian Stock Exchange and does not involve human subjects, animals, personal data, or clinical samples
declarations.funderStatement: The author is the founder and CEO of Metricon LLC, which operates the quarterly beta refresh described in this paper as part of the Quarterly Research module of its financial-data subscription product. No external party funded, reviewed, or approved the methodology prior to public disclosure.

detail.abstract: The Capital Asset Pricing Model beta is the workhorse measure of systematic risk in equity finance, yet the default Bloomberg/MSCI calibration-five years of weekly returns against a broad market index-was developed for and remains tuned to deep, liquid, developed-country equity markets. Direct transplantation to a frontier market such as the Mongolian Stock Exchange (MSE, MIC: XULA) produces biased and uninterpretable estimates: sparse trading creates stale-price contamination, the median listed firm trades fewer than three times per week, free-float scarcity inflates idiosyncratic variance, and survivorship-corrected listing histories are too short to support the standard five-year window. This paper specifies a frontier-market-native beta methodology calibrated on three explicit design choices-(i) a three-year rolling window of weekly Friday-close ISO-week samples, (ii) the TOP-20 capitalisation-weighted index as market proxy, (iii) a 60-raw-trade-day / 30-weekly-observation eligibility floor-and applies it to all 161 currently-listed MSE common shares. We document four central findings: (1) all seven sector portfolios exhibit beta strictly below unity (βsector = 0.49, ticker-weighted); (2) explanatory power R 2 exceeds 0.20 for only one ticker (Golomt Bank, R 2 = 0.246) and is below 0.05 for the median listed firm; (3) negative beta estimates appear in fourteen tickers but in every case carry R 2 < 0.015 and are statistically indistinguishable from zero; (4) Bloomberg-style Vasicek shrinkage toward a sector-conditional prior-rather than the conventional 1.0 prior-would alter median ticker beta by approximately 12 percentage points. We then integrate our β estimates with the country-level ERP from Damodaran (2023) to produce CAPM cost-of-equity estimates for the high-R 2 subuniverse, and adopt the Damodaran multi-method cross-validation discipline at the firm-level by reporting OLS, Vasicek, Dimson sumbeta, and sector-portfolio betas side-by-side. The framework is in continuous production use at Metricon and is refreshed quarterly; full replication artefacts are provided.

title: Green skepticism in vertically differentiated markets: competition, environmental quality, and welfare
affiliations: University of Toulon

detail.title: Green skepticism in vertically differentiated markets: competition, environmental quality, and welfare
detail.abstract: We study how green skepticism --- the systematic underestimation of green product quality by a fraction of consumers --- shapes market competition, environmental quality, and welfare. In a vertical differentiation duopoly, confident consumers correctly perceive product qualities while skeptical consumers underestimate the green product. We characterize skepticism along two dimensions: its degree and its share. When the degree is intermediate and the share is sufficiently large, perceived product differentiation collapses, price competition intensifies, and the market falls into an \textit{environmental trap}: a brown monopoly that yields the worst environmental outcome and the lowest profits for both firms. The effects of skepticism are non-monotonic: both firms can benefit when skepticism is strong but confined to a minority, and environmental quality can improve when green production costs are high. Welfare implications depend on whether welfare is evaluated using perceived or actual qualities, generating a trade-off between economic efficiency and environmental protection. A combination of a green subsidy financed by a brown tax, a stricter ecolabel, and a green product quota can address this trade-off.

title: The Foundations of an Appropriate Price Theory
affiliations: Universitas Prasetiya Mulya - School of Business and Economics

detail.title: The Foundations of an Appropriate Price Theory
detail.abstract: This article develops the foundations of an appropriate price theory by restoring prices to their central role as institutions of social coordination, economic calculation, interpretation, and entrepreneurial discovery. Moving beyond the view of prices as mere numerical variables or policy targets, it argues that prices emerge from subjective valuation, voluntary exchange, private property, and institutional conditions that allow dispersed knowledge to become socially usable. Drawing on Menger, Mises, Hayek, Huerta de Soto, Chicago price theory, evolutionary economics, and hermeneutical political economy, the article presents prices as relative, calculational, epistemic, entrepreneurial, and evolutionary signals. It stresses that prices guide production and consumption under scarcity, uncertainty, and structural change, while also disciplining error through profit and loss. The paper concludes that a renewed price theory is essential not only for economic analysis, but also as a safeguard against policy illusions that suppress price signals and misunderstand the complexity of market processes

title: Zero Tolerance or Strong Cultural Diversity: The Hard Case of Female Genital Surgery
affiliations: University of Kentucky  and University of Kentucky, College of Law

detail.title: Zero Tolerance or Strong Cultural Diversity: The Hard Case of Female Genital Surgery
detail.abstract:
This article applies a thesis favoring strong cultural diversity to defend a subject-centered policy regarding female genital surgeries (FGS). That idea posits that cultural variation holds an intrinsic value that should be presumptively respected when setting policy and creating law. Correlatively, cultural homogenization, especially by force, should be resisted.

Taking as a starting point the recent celebration of the United Nation’s Day of Zero-Tolerance for Female Genital Mutilation, the paper reviews the context of FGS practices in various societies and critiques the inconsistencies of U.N. arguments to advance its goal of total elimination by 2030. Especially problematic for the U.N. rhetoric depicting the evils of FGS are the facts that comparable surgeries provided to American women go uncriticized, and that while female genital surgeries of any kind are often criminalized, comparable procedures on males are legally shielded, as happened recently in Germany.

Despite the enormous expenditure and effort exerted by the United Nations, its strategy has resulted in only incremental decreases in the practice. What it has accomplished, however, has been to shame and disparage a great number of women.

We recommend a middle course, one built on the expressed priorities of the women involved: that the procedure be relocated into a medical setting to minimize health sequelae that can accompany any surgery, with informed consent. More importantly, however, we urge that attention be given to the underlying factors to which FGS is but a response. Greater work to improve the economic and social prospects for women would reduce much of the pressure for a woman to find a suitable husband and financial security via a proven gateway, one which the West has arbitrarily identified as the world’s most severe human rights violation.

title: Scale, Delusion, and the Funding of Entrepreneurial Ventures A Model of Effort, Over-Optimism, and Welfare
affiliations: UCLA Anderson and

detail.title: Scale, Delusion, and the Funding of Entrepreneurial Ventures A Model of Effort, Over-Optimism, and Welfare
detail.abstract: We develop a model of entrepreneurial venture creation in which founders hold systematically upward-biased beliefs about project returns. A project of scale 𝑋 succeeds with probability 𝜋(𝑒), increasing in effort, and yields 𝐾𝑋; the entrepreneur believes the payoff is Δ𝐾𝑋 where Δ > 1. She raises external capital 𝐸 in exchange for an equity stake, priced rationally by investors, and bears a fixed personal cost 𝜅 of founding with a non-contractible component 𝜅 𝑛. The central result is that entrepreneurial delusion amplifies effort by exactly the factor Δ relative to the social optimum, generating a deadweight welfare loss proportional to (Δ-1) 2 and to 𝑋 2. The funding geometry has four regimes determined by two thresholds: a minimum viable scale 𝑋 min above which actual welfare is non-negative, and a participation threshold 𝑋 del above which the deluded entrepreneur willingly engages. When non-contractible costs are small, 𝑋 del < 𝑋 min and the binding constraint is welfare; the deluded entrepreneur enters socially destructive ventures (the Funding Trap). When non-contractible costs are large, 𝑋 del > 𝑋 min and the binding constraint is participation; even deluded founders refuse socially valuable ventures (the Participation Gap). Delusion is thus a conditional blessing: harmful in low-𝜅 𝑛 environments and helpful in high-𝜅 𝑛 environments, by precisely the dual margin of pulling the entrepreneur into more-or fewer-ventures than a rational agent would attempt.

title: Optimal Carbon Payments and Adoption Under Soil Carbon Sequestration: An Analytical Characterization

detail.title: Optimal Carbon Payments and Adoption Under Soil Carbon Sequestration: An Analytical Characterization
detail.abstract: This paper derives closed-form expressions for carbon payment schemes that incentivize the adoption of conservation tillage for soil carbon sequestration. The analytical results closely match those obtained from a stochastic Markov decision process framework, while offering the advantage of mathematically precise relationships between payment design and underlying parameters. The analysis reveals that minimum carbon payments decline sharply as the sequestration rate accelerates, underscoring the importance of promoting technologies that speed up carbon accumulation as a policy lever. Optimal payments vary significantly across soil types. Flat payment schemes result in long breakeven periods, whereas front-loaded schemes can substantially shorten the breakeven horizon. The framework yields conditions that guarantee incentive-compatibility for the latter class of schemes as the payment stream diminishes over time.

title:
From Manifest Destiny to Maduro: Two Centuries of American Wild West 
How America's Founding Mythology Continues to Justify Imperial Violence

detail.title:
From Manifest Destiny to Maduro: Two Centuries of American Wild West 
How America's Founding Mythology Continues to Justify Imperial Violence
detail.abstract: This paper examines the January 2026 U.S. military operation to arrest Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro as the latest manifestation of a structural logic dating to America's nineteenth-century "Wild West" expansion. Through analysis of primary historical sources from the Library of Congress (1847-1899 newspapers), the article demonstrates continuities in American imperial practice: delegitimizing targeted populations, inverting agency to portray aggressors as victims, and prioritizing resource extraction under shifting ideological justifications. The analysis employs a non-Western theoretical framework drawing on Ibn Khaldun's concept of 'asabiyya (social cohesion/legitimacy) and Malik Bennabi's theory of qabiliyya li-l-isti'mar (colonizability) to argue that Trump's Venezuela operation—and his frank admission to "engage heavily in Venezuelan oil"—represents not deviation but return to foundational American logic, now stripped of liberal pretenses. The article concludes that this return to "naked force" without legitimacy signals not imperial strength but terminal decline, following patterns Ibn Khaldun identified in empires across Islamic history. Keywords: American empire, Wild West, Manifest Destiny, Venezuela, Trump, Ibn Khaldun, Malik Bennabi, imperialism, legitimacy crisis

title: Transforming Landscapes: The Impact of China's Grain for Green Program on Agricultural Productivity
affiliations: Wesleyan University, Fudan University,  and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

detail.title: Transforming Landscapes: The Impact of China's Grain for Green Program on Agricultural Productivity
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of the Grain for Green Program, one of the largest Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) programs in the world, on agricultural productivity. We develop a conceptual framework with frictional land markets to analyze how the program affects rural households' labor and land allocation decisions and the resulting productivity outcomes. Our empirical findings support the model's predictions. Specifically, the program significantly increased rural households' efficient labor allocation to off-farm employment, particularly among households with low initial agricultural productivity. The program also corrected land misallocation across households and promoted land consolidation and technology upgrading. Through the combined effects of labor sorting, cross-household land reallocation, and technology upgrading, the program raised average agricultural productivity in treated villages by approximately 2.6%.

title: The Political Economy Dimensions of Macroeconomic Management of Aid in Ghana
affiliations: University of Ghana,  and Centre for Social Policy Studies, University of Ghana

detail.title: The Political Economy Dimensions of Macroeconomic Management of Aid in Ghana
detail.abstract: This paper contributes to the debate on aid effectiveness by looking at the 'how' of aid effectiveness. In other words it provides an assessment of whether aid only filled a financing gap or whether it, in addition, helped influence the political economy in a way that engendered growth. Ghana provides a good case for an assessment of this question as it saw significant aid inflows over the last two and a half decades and also recorded significant growth and poverty reduction. The paper asserts that aid has impacted positively on growth, in part through the creation of an enabling environment for private sector-led growth. It also argues that aid has helped shape macroeconomic management in Ghana, identifying three channels through which aid has supported macroeconomic management. First, aid has supported both physical and social infrastructure and therefore growth. Second, aid has helped reduce fiscal instability by limiting domestic borrowing. Third, it helped shape the general policy direction in Ghana. It concludes by arguing that the aid-induced policy has helped in the operation of a more effective and efficient market system in Ghana today.

title: Stoic Capitalism? Adam Smith versus Marcus Aurelius
affiliations: University of Central Florida

detail.title: Stoic Capitalism? Adam Smith versus Marcus Aurelius
detail.abstract: Is there a common thread that unites Marcus Aurelius’ devotion to cooperation and the common good and Adam Smith’s celebration of self-interest into a logically coherent and soul-cleansing whole? Is Stoic virtue compatible with the pursuit of profit, or do markets, to paraphrase Michael J. Sandel, “crowd out” morality? My contribution to this discussion is to reconcile Marcus Aurelius’ Meditations and Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations. To this end, the remainder of my paper is organized as follows: Part II provides some historical background into what I call the “Stoic-capitalist dilemma,” i.e. the tension between Stoic ethics and capitalist self-interest. Next, Part III explains why Stoic ideals and the capitalist ethos, despite some overlaps and points of intersection, are fundamentally at odds with each other. Part IV, however, proposes a novel solution to the Stoic-capitalist dilemma: I introduce Adam Smith’s “impartial spectator” and then re-conceptualize Smith’s imaginary observer as a Stoic sage or “inner Marcus Aurelius” inside each one of us. Part V then anticipates some criticisms of my Stoic interpretation of Smith’s impartial spectator device and concludes with some suggestions for further research.

title: Institutions and the transmission of upper-tail human capital: scientific lineages across a millennium
affiliations: Meisei University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Hitotsubashi University - Institute of Innovation Research

detail.title: Institutions and the transmission of upper-tail human capital: scientific lineages across a millennium
detail.abstract: What made useful knowledge cumulative was not discovery alone but the institutions that transmitted it. We provide the first exhaustive structural measurement of the network through which upper-tail human capital passed from master to student across a millennium. Using 470,000 mentor--student records from Wikidata (which integrates the Mathematics Genealogy Project and MacTutor Archive), and all 64 historical Fields Medalists as a fixed, ex ante tracer set, backward traversal yields a directed acyclic graph of 25.5 million paths reaching 57 generations. We document two institutional transitions. First, a 17th-century watershed concentrates lineage traffic on Leibniz: 47 of 64 lineages pass through him with a 10:1 downstream-to-upstream ratio, and seven independent attributes---learned-society membership (a 46-fold rise per scholar), field, language, employer, institutional diversification, student production, and diffusion entropy---re-organize coherently across the samewindow. This is the network signature of Mokyr's Republic of Letters, and it reframes the Newton--Leibniz priority dispute as a distinction between the possession and the transmission of upper-tail human capital: it is transmission that generates the spillovers on which growth depends. Second, 84% of lineages converge upstream on five 12th--13th-century Islamic and Byzantine scholars before terminating at an 11th-century boundary---the ''Monastery Wall''---at which personal academic mentorship first becomes record-generating in Europe. Our claims are descriptive-structural, not causal. Because exhaustive traversal at this scale defeats standard tools, we also contribute a deterministic, algebraic graph-traversal instrument whose measurement bias we characterize in closed form, and report one emergent property of independent methodological interest.

title: U.S. Defense and Security Aid and Hidden Money in Offshore Bank Accounts
affiliations: KU Eichstaett-Ingolstadt - Department of Economics and Business Administration

detail.title: U.S. Defense and Security Aid and Hidden Money in Offshore Bank Accounts
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether U.S. defense and security aid is systematically diverted by recipient-country elites into offshore bank accounts. I combine project-level data on U.S. defense and security aid disbursements from 2013-2018 with bilateral crossborder bank deposit data from the Bank for International Settlements. Exploiting within-country variation, I find that deposits held in high-secrecy offshore jurisdictions increase in quarters with U.S. defense and security aid disbursements, while deposits in other international financial centers do not. However, this relationship is not broad-based across recipient countries. Instead, it is driven by a small number of countries receiving exceptionally large aid disbursements and by quarters in which aid exceeds high thresholds relative to GDP. In contrast, U.S. economic and development aid is not associated with comparable offshore deposit dynamics. The findings suggest that while elite capture can occur in high-intensity settings, diversion of U.S. defense and security aid is not a structural phenomenon.

title: The Gains of Inter-Firm Cooperation Among Micro Entreprises in Selected Leather Industrial Clusters in Nigeria
affiliations: Redeemer's University - Department of Business Administration and Marketing and Department of Financial Studies, Redeemers University

detail.title: The Gains of Inter-Firm Cooperation Among Micro Entreprises in Selected Leather Industrial Clusters in Nigeria
detail.abstract: The policy on local content and consumption of locally produced goods in Nigeria is expected to improve the competitiveness of indigenous businesses and contribute to the growth of the nation's economy. However, the co-location of firms is a critical factor in firm cooperation, and developed nations have already established an environment for firms to colocate and cooperate. This study aimed to investigate the co-location of firms and the gains of inter-firm cooperation, with a focus on the spatial proximity of firms and the benefits enjoyed by MSMEs when they collaborate. To achieve the study's purpose, the multistage sampling methods with survey design were employed. The study analyzed the results of three clusters and examined the gains MSMEs receive from inter-firm cooperation using the descriptive and regression analyses. The study found that business growth (t = 4.145; p = 0.000) was the most significant gain of inter-firm cooperation according to two out of the three clusters studied. Also, cooperation gains have significant influence on marketing cooperation, Research & Development cooperation, and Innovation (f= p<0.001) in the leather industrial clusters in Nigeria. The study concluded that an enabling environment for business growth, access to information, and other supportive factors could drive inter-firm collaboration in Nigeria's leather industry. To compete in the global market, Nigerian businesses must adopt strategies that foster inter-firm cooperation and take lessons from the co-location of firms in developed nations.

title: Dollar, Eurodollar, and the Myths of Petrodollar and De-dollarisation
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dollar, Eurodollar, and the Myths of Petrodollar and De-dollarisation
detail.abstract:
Since the attack on Iran by Israel and the United States (US) that began on 28 February 2026, there

has been intense debate regarding petrodollar and dedollarisation. Our objective in this brief

note—based on publicly available data—is to show that there has been no such thing as the

petrodollar, and that although the US dollar's dominance has been eroding for some time, the world

has not yet reached a point of global dedollarisation. In what follows, we begin with the US return

to the gold standard in 1879, which laid the foundation for how the dollar overtook the pound

sterling to become the dominant reserve and trade currency. We then emphasise the significance

of the eurodollar market that emerged in the early 1950s, while tracing the evolution since 1879.

title: Causal Identification of Bid-Ask Spread Components: A Double Machine Learning Approach

detail.title: Causal Identification of Bid-Ask Spread Components: A Double Machine Learning Approach
detail.abstract: Although market microstructure researchers have long associated bid-ask spread widening during volatile episodes with elevated adverse selection risk, this attribution is substantially overstated. The overstatement is most severe precisely where accurate measurement is most consequential. By applying the Double Machine Learning (DML) framework of Chernozhukov et al. (2018) to five-minute OHLCV bars for Apple Inc. over Q2 2024, the results demonstrate that causal estimates of the adverse selection component are three to five times smaller than Huang-Stoll Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimates across all volatility regimes. I identified that realized volatility simultaneously widens spreads and generates large price movements, and OLS conflates this mechanical correlation with genuine information asymmetry. DML removes this confound through cross-fitted gradient boosting nuisance models that partial out intraday determinants of both the spread and the price impact proxy before the final causal regression. The adverse selection component, measured by the absolute one-period forward mid-price return, exhibits a statistically significant and monotonically increasing causal effect of θ̂ = 7.37 (low volatility), 12.14 (medium), and 19.39 (high), with Huang-Stoll overstatement ratios of 4.9×, 3.3×, and 5.0× respectively. The inventory component is causally inert in all regimes once confounders are removed. Results are robust to alternative trade signing via Bulk Volume Classification and to relative spread normalization. These findings have direct implications for regulatory cost-of-trading assessments and academic studies of information asymmetry that rely on structural decomposition estimates as data inputs.

title: A Machine Learning Framework for Human Capital-Based Mortgage Qualification: Evidence from U.S. Immigrant Borrower Cohorts

detail.title: A Machine Learning Framework for Human Capital-Based Mortgage Qualification: Evidence from U.S. Immigrant Borrower Cohorts
detail.abstract: Traditional FICO-based mortgage underwriting systematically excludes recently arrived immigrants who lack domestic credit history, even when their income, educational credentials, and housing payment behaviour indicate strong creditworthiness. This study applies a Random Forest machine learning framework to develop and validate the Human Capital Wealth Capacity Index (HC-WCI), an AI-augmented alternative qualification tool built on three publicly observable variables: educational attainment, years of U.S. residency, and a geospatially normalised Rent Performance Ratio. Using American Community Survey (ACS) microdata covering 166 million weighted person-observations across ten immigrant national-origin groups, a four-model machine learning comparison shows that human capital variables explain 14.0% of cohort-level mortgage rate variation, compared with 5.6% for income alone. Two supplementary datasets are used to validate the framework's central claims. American Housing Survey (AHS) 2023 data confirm that renters in the highest Rent Performance Ratio quartile face a late payment rate of 4.65%, compared with 8.64% in the lowest quartile (χ²=59.73, p<0.001). Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) data from 2016 to 2022 show that credit exclusion rates fall monotonically from 29.6% among households with some high school education to 8.5% among college graduates. Together, the findings provide an empirical foundation for incorporating machine learning-derived human capital signals into U.S. mortgage underwriting and offer a practical AI-assisted pre-screening tool for identifying credit-invisible immigrant households that current models systematically misclassify.

title: When Aggregation Obscures: Evidence from SG&A Disaggregation
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School, Pennsylvania State University and Arizona State University (ASU)

detail.title: When Aggregation Obscures: Evidence from SG&A Disaggregation
detail.abstract: Financial statements necessarily aggregate underlying transactions into broad reporting categories. Although aggregation helps summarize complex business activity, it may also obscure meaningful differences if line items combine activities with differing implications for future performance and valuation. We examine this issue in the context of selling, general, and administrative (SG&A) expense, which commonly combines selling and marketing (S&M) expenditures with general and administrative (G&A) expenditures. Using granular XBRL filings that preserve more detailed reporting information than traditional commercial databases, we find that more than a quarter of firms separately report S&M and G&A on the face of the income statement. We use these disclosures to examine whether S&M and G&A exhibit distinct economic properties. Our findings reveal that S&M is positively associated with firm value, whereas G&A is negatively associated. S&M is also more strongly associated with future revenue than G&A. Finally, S&M and G&A exhibit different patterns of cost adjustment, with S&M displaying anti-sticky behavior that is obscured when the two components are combined into aggregate SG&A. Overall, our evidence suggests that disaggregating SG&A reveals economically meaningful information that is not evident in aggregate SG&A. These findings speak to recent investor and standard-setter interest in expense disaggregation by showing that separating SG&A into functional components reveals economically meaningful information not evident in aggregate SG&A.

title: Bellgrid: GPU-Native Backward Induction for Stochastic Dynamic Programs with Mixed Continuous and Discrete State and Action Spaces
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Bellgrid: GPU-Native Backward Induction for Stochastic Dynamic Programs with Mixed Continuous and Discrete State and Action Spaces
detail.abstract: We present bellgrid, a GPU-native solver for discrete-time stochastic dynamic programs (DPs) over state and action spaces that may freely mix continuous, discrete-categorical, and Markov-chain components. The Bellman recursion is evaluated by backward induction over a user-chosen state mesh, integrating expectations by quadrature rules selected per shock type (Gauss-Hermite for Gaussian and lognormal innovations, Cholesky-rotated tensor-product Gauss-Hermite for multivariate Gaussians, Gauss-Legendre for uniforms, exact summation for finite-support distributions, and Bernoulli arrivals with Gauss-Hermite magnitudes for Mertonian jumps), and interpolating the continuation value multilinearly at next-state coordinates with exact gather on discrete and Markov-chain components. The same Problem specification supports finite-and infinite-horizon problems, scalar or state-dependent discount factors, and per-period rewards that may optionally depend on the realised next state. We validate the solver on nine canonical problems-a log-utility Merton consumptionportfolio model, Carroll-Deaton lifecycle savings with a borrowing constraint, an American put under geometric Brownian motion, a 2-D linear-quadratic-Gaussian control problem, two-asset Merton with correlated returns, an American put under regime-switching volatility, a discrete retirement decision, an American put under Merton (1976) jump diffusion, and a full lifecycle planning model with mortality, warm-glow bequest, and regime-switching markets-against analytical or numerical references in every case; agreement is to machine precision for the closed-form cases and within 10-4 to 10-3 otherwise. On a single RTX 6000 Ada the full lifecycle problem (∼1.2 billion Bellman cell-action-shock evaluations end to end) solves in 1.8 seconds, a 45× speedup over the same code on a 32-core CPU. bellgrid is released as an open-source Python package under the MIT license.

title: The Uneven Frontier: User Heterogeneity and the External Validity of Language Model Benchmarks
affiliations: Equitech Futures

detail.title: The Uneven Frontier: User Heterogeneity and the External Validity of Language Model Benchmarks
detail.abstract: Benchmarks treat language model quality as a property of the model. But what users actually experience is jointly produced by the model and the user; and users differ enormously in how skillfully they prompt, evaluate outputs, and choose which problems to bring to AI in the first place. This paper develops a framework for what follows from that fact. We define the quality surface: a landscape over input space whose peaks and valleys are established by the prompt-sensitivity literature. Users navigate this surface with skill-dependent strategies, producing an elicitation divergence. Experienced quality diverges across the population over time, even when everyone uses the same model. We prove that this divergence causes benchmark rankings to lose their predictive power for population outcomes, with rank reversal between models emerging as a special case under empirically realistic conditions. Our framework also reconciles a puzzle in the AI productivity literature: short, constrained tasks compress the productivity distribution and help low-skill workers most, while long, open-ended deployments with task-selection discretion let high-skill workers pull ahead. Both patterns fall out of the same dynamics under different parameters. We propose an elicitability index that measures how much a model's quality depends on user skill, separating forces that reduce this dependence (RLHF, instruction tuning) from forces that amplify it (capability growth, agentic mediation). We establish these results formally and illustrate them through simulations, and we outline an empirical validation strategy using public conversation corpora. The framework names what we call elicitation inequality: users with identical access to the same model can experience it as qualitatively different technologies, depending on how they navigate it. This is a new and currently unmeasured dimension of digital inequality, and it changes what evaluation has to measure, what deployment has to account for, and what governance has to address.

title: Strategic Attacks, Network Losses, and Cascading Failures
affiliations: University of Florida, University of Florida - Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering and University of Florida

detail.title: Strategic Attacks, Network Losses, and Cascading Failures
detail.abstract: This paper investigates strategic attacks in a network of interconnected agents subject to cascading losses. We develop a damage-maximization framework to identify disruption strategies that amplify systemic losses. Each agent is endowed with an initial capital level that determines its resilience. Losses arise endogenously from defaulted neighbors and exogenously through direct attacks. We consider a dynamic linear-threshold contagion model in which agents default when shocks and contagious losses drive their capital below a critical level. We present three linear attack models. The first two assume complete information about the network topology: one imposes an overall attack budget, while the other enforces period-specific budgets. For both models, we identify structural properties of optimal solutions and formulate them as valid and super valid inequalities. Computational experiments on financial and supplychain networks show that these inequalities significantly accelerate solution times as network scale increases. The third model assumes incomplete information and allows us to quantify the value of information in shaping optimal attack strategies and systemic risk assessment.

title: Global Equity Risk Premiums (ERP) & Country Risk Premiums (CRP)

detail.title: Global Equity Risk Premiums (ERP) & Country Risk Premiums (CRP)
detail.abstract: Every valuation rests on a discount rate, and every discount rate rests on a risk premium. When that valuation involves a company operating in Brazil or an acquirer pricing a target in Indonesia, the question of which risk premium to use becomes anything but trivial, investors in these markets bear political instability, violence, corruption, and institutional fragility that mature markets have largely priced away. Ignoring that is not conservatism, it is mispricing. This paper documents the methodology for estimating Equity Risk Premiums and Country Risk Premiums across 174 countries and 9 global regions as of April-May 2026, building explicitly on the framework developed by Professor Aswath Damodaran of NYU Stern, with three methodological refinements: the risk-free rate is derived by netting CDS spreads against Switzerland rather than applying a rating-based default spread, ensuring consistency with the CRP framework; the mature market ERP strips America's full country risk premium rather than its raw sovereign default spread from the implied ERP; the relative volatility multiplier uses indices with balanced exposure across both developed and emerging markets; all through a three-tier hierarchy of CDS spreads, Moody's rating-implied spreads, and Political Risk Service scores. The result is a set of estimates any analyst can use in cross-border valuation without rebuilding the methodology from scratch.
