detail.title: Structural Divergence and the Crisis of Institutional Alignment in advanced Democracies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. No funding was received for this research. The author is the founder of the Convergent Society project, which is referenced in the paper, but this relationship does not constitute a financial competing interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Across advanced democratic societies, many citizens are living through deteriorating conditions that the vocabulary applied to explaining policy failures cannot adequately describe. This paper argues that the simultaneous deterioration of institutional trust, democratic satisfaction, social connection, economic security, and epistemic coherence in the same societies over the same period is better understood as the manifestation of a shared structural condition-Structural Divergence-than as a convergence of independent failures. At the institutional level, this condition is produced by structural incoherence: the breakdown of alignment among the governing logics of economic, political, social, and epistemic subsystems, generated through the compounding processes of institutional drift and capture. We establish the empirical case through three tests: the duration of trends that predate commonly cited shocks; their cross-national consistency across different institutional arrangements; and the Performance-Experience Asymmetry between continued system performance and deteriorating citizen experience. A small cluster of advanced democracies-Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Switzerland-appears consistently as exceptions, and their institutional architecture provides the comparative evidence for what coherencemaintaining arrangements require. The paper identifies five directions for future empirical research and concludes with implications for institutional design, civic capacity, and the possibility of convergence.

title: Differences in Parenting Styles Between Adolescent and Adult Mothers: A Comparative Analysis in an Iranian Setting
affiliations: Ardabil University of Medical Sciences, Ardabil University of Medical Sciences and Ardebil University of Medical Sciences

detail.title: Differences in Parenting Styles Between Adolescent and Adult Mothers: A Comparative Analysis in an Iranian Setting
detail.abstract: Parenting style is one of the key factors in children's psychological, social, and physical development. This concept encompasses a set of parental attitudes toward their child that are transmitted to the child and create an emotional environment in which parental behaviors are expressed. The aim of this study was to determine the differences in parenting styles between adolescent and adult mothers in Ardabil city. In this cross-sectional analytical study, 600 eligible mothers (300 adolescents and 300 adults) were selected and included in the study by random cluster sampling from comprehensive health centers in Ardabil city, in 2025. Data were collected with a demographic and Baumrind questionnaire (30 questions). Data analysis was performed with descriptive tests, chi-square, ANOVA, Pearson correlation, and multivariate regression in SPSS version 24 software. The results showed that adolescent mothers had a higher score in the permissive style (1.44±0.69) and a lower score in the authoritarian style (1.68±0.66) than adult mothers (1.09± 0.71) and (1.9±0.66) (p<0.01). The mean total parenting score was lower in adolescent mothers (2.09±0.19) vs. (2.05±0.20) p=0.005). Multiple regression showed that increasing maternal age was associated with an improvement in the total parenting score and increasing age at marriage was associated with a decrease (β=-0.189, p=0.011). Adolescent mothers have less supportive and more permissive parenting styles, and early marriage is associated with a decrease in the quality of parenting. Special educational and support programs for teenage mothers can improve the quality of parenting practices.

title: When and How to Schedule in Real-time
affiliations: , Technische Universität München (TUM) and Technische Universität München (TUM)

detail.title: When and How to Schedule in Real-time

declarations.funderStatement: SAP SE financially supported this research under the contract number IPA(DE-2021-076)

detail.abstract: Real-time scheduling approaches respond to dynamic uncertainties, such as varying processing times, in smart manufacturing systems. This paper investigates the conditions under which realtime scheduling yields performance benefits over static plans. We focus on flexible flow shops with non-identical parallel machines and sequence-dependent setup times, reflecting real-world complexity. The scheduling problem is modeled as a Markov Decision Process that captures job-machine allocations. While existing literature primarily links the value of real-time scheduling to the level of uncertainty, we extend this perspective by examining the impact of system characteristics, i.e., the number of parallel machines, their heterogeneity, and the heterogeneity in setup times. Our results show that real-time scheduling benefits from greater routing flexibility, but its benefits decline when machine and setup-time heterogeneity create assignment and sequencing structures that restrict allocation flexibility. We further validate our approach in a real-world case study in food manufacturing, where allowing machines to remain idle proves critical for performance. To provide insights on how to schedule in real-time, we compare three prominent solution approaches: (i) Constraint Programming, which creates static lookahead schedules that are continuously rescheduled; (ii) Deep Reinforcement Learning, which trains state-dependent decisions through large-scale simulation; and (iii) Genetic Programming, which uses simulation to learn decision rules. For medium to very large stochastic instances, our enhanced Genetic Programming approach achieves the strongest overall performance among the tested real-time methods and outperforms the static scheduling benchmark.

title: From Khaldunian Sociology to Administrative Engineering: A Structural Dialectical Analysis of Tribal Solidarity (Asabiyyah) in Emerging Political Systems
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Khaldunian Sociology to Administrative Engineering: A Structural Dialectical Analysis of Tribal Solidarity (Asabiyyah) in Emerging Political Systems
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a dual theoretical framework that integrates Khaldunian historical sociology with Weberian institutional analysis to examine the structural dynamics of emerging and transitional political systems. Drawing on the concepts of Asabiyyah in the work of Ibn Khaldun and the theory of legitimacy and bureaucratic rationalization in the work of Max Weber, the study proposes an analytical model that explains state formation as a layered process in which social cohesion and institutional structuring operate simultaneously rather than sequentially.
The research addresses a central gap in political sociology: the tendency of
classical Weberian frameworks to overemphasize formal-legal rationality while
under-theorizing the informal, solidarity-based structures that shape real
patterns of authority in transitional contexts. Conversely, Khaldunian theory
provides a dynamic account of social cohesion and political ascent but lacks a
formalized account of bureaucratic stabilization mechanisms. By bridging these
two traditions, the paper conceptualizes political authority as a dual structure
composed of a generative social engine (Asabiyyah) and a stabilizing
institutional layer (bureaucracy).
Methodologically, the study adopts a structural-dialectical approach that
combines comparative political sociology with conceptual modeling. It
operationalizes key variables such as social cohesion, legitimacy type
distribution, and administrative rationalization to construct a preliminary
framework for analyzing hybrid governance systems in the Middle East and
North Africa.
The paper argues that transitional political systems are best understood not as
incomplete modern states, but as structurally hybrid formations in which
Khaldunian and Weberian logics coexist, overlap, and continuously reshape
each other. This duality provides a more accurate explanatory model for
institutional resilience, fragmentation, and cyclical transformation in
contemporary political orders.

title: When Directors Need Direction: Whom Do Board Members Go to for Advice?
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, The Miles Group (TMG), Stanford University and Stanford University - Graduate School of Business

detail.title: When Directors Need Direction: Whom Do Board Members Go to for Advice?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rock Center for Corporate Governance at Stanford University Working Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Rock Center for Corporate Governance at Stanford University Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
In this Closer Look, we examine the formal and informal advice networks that corporate directors rely on to improve decision making and performance. We find directors are active consumers of advice. They rely on paid advisors particularly in their early years to acquire new skills as they learn to oversee management and function in a boardroom setting. They turn to unpaid advisors to formulate viewpoints on big picture questions of strategy, culture, and governance—applying the best of the insights from both sources to improve corporate outcomes. While traditional governance models typically view directors as independent experts who bring their own skills and experience to the board room, the evidence suggests directors may function as nodes in broader networks of information and expertise.

We ask:

·       How much is director effectiveness determined by individual knowledge versus knowledge they access through personal and professional networks?

·       How should researchers think about the value of a director's network as a form of social capital?

·       How should boards think about the quality of a director candidate’s network during the recruitment process?

·       Under what circumstances do advice networks improve decision quality, and when might they create risks of groupthink, conflicts of interest, or information leakage?

title: Operational Responsibility in AI Governance: A User-centric Liability Framework
affiliations: University of Northern Iowa - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics

detail.title: Operational Responsibility in AI Governance: A User-centric Liability Framework
detail.abstract: Who bears responsibility when artificial intelligence systems cause harm? This question has become central to AI ethics and governance. Most existing approaches focus on developers, yet this faces serious practical and theoretical problems. Drawing on tort law, agency law, and philosophy of technology, this paper argues that AI should be understood as an instrument whose outputs remain the responsibility of human operators rather than developers. We call this 'usercentric governance.' Placing accountability with deployers promotes public trust by creating clear lines of responsibility, a concern that governance approaches have often overlooked. It preserves democratic accountability by keeping human actors answerable for AI-mediated decisions, and it counters power imbalances by ensuring that those who use AI bear consequences for how they use it. Legal principles of instrumentality show that operational responsibility should follow use rather than creation. We propose a 'distributed yet centered' governance model that acknowledges developer obligations while treating deployment decisions as the center of primary accountability.

title: Human Capital Investment and Digital Transformation: A Complementarity Argument for Strategic Social Skill Development.

detail.title: Human Capital Investment and Digital Transformation: A Complementarity Argument for Strategic Social Skill Development.
detail.abstract: The relationship between human resource investment and technological transformation has been theorised predominantly through a reactive lens: organisations develop workforce capabilities in response to technological change. This paper challenges that framing by advancing a complementarity argument, namely that structured investment in social skill development constitutes a strategically prior condition for effective technological adoption rather than a subsequent accommodation to it. Drawing on human capital theory (Becker, 1964), socio-technical systems perspectives (Trist, 1981), and service-dominant logic (Vargo and Lusch, 2008), the paper develops a conceptual framework in which social skills (encompassing interpersonal communication, collaborative problem-solving, and emotional intelligence) function as enabling complements to technological capability rather than residual human functions. Empirical grounding is provided by a survey-based exploratory study (n = 104) of UK-based employees across multiple industries, conducted in 2023, which consistently found that participants perceived structured HR skill development as positively associated with workforce adaptability, organisational performance, and individual career progression. The paper contributes a theoretically integrated argument to contemporary debates on augmentation versus substitution in AI-enabled work environments, and identifies directions for future longitudinal and comparative empirical research. While the findings are exploratory and the sample subject to the known limitations of convenience sampling, the conceptual argument has implications for strategic HRM practice and for the theoretical positioning of social skill investment within broader frameworks of organisational capability development.

title: Defanging the Nanny State
affiliations: Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA)

detail.title: Defanging the Nanny State
detail.abstract:
Defanging the Nanny State (IEA Discussion Paper No. 131, December 2024) by Dr Christopher Snowdon examines the case against coercive paternalism in British public policy and sets out a practical reform agenda for rolling back lifestyle regulation. Drawing on the IEA's biennial Nanny State Index, a league table measuring the restrictiveness of government regulation across food, alcohol, soft drinks, tobacco, and nicotine products in 30 European countries, Snowdon argues that the UK has long ranked among the most interventionist nations in Europe, despite the public health lobby's portrayal of the British government as insufficiently bold.

The paper challenges the key justifications for paternalistic regulation, showing that so-called "sin taxes" are deeply regressive, falling disproportionately on lower-income households with little demonstrable benefit to their health. It further contends that coercive measures consistently fail on their own terms: because demand for the targeted products tends to be inelastic, significant intrusions on consumer freedom are required to achieve even modest behavioural change. Meanwhile, countries at the bottom of the Nanny State Index, such as Germany and the Czech Republic, show no worse health outcomes than those in the UK and, in several cases, have higher life expectancy.

Rather than advocating a wholesale libertarian dismantling of all regulation, the paper sets a defined and achievable goal: to identify the policy changes needed to make the UK the freest country in Europe for lifestyle choices, matching or slightly bettering Germany's score on the Index. Snowdon outlines concrete reforms across sin taxes, advertising restrictions, product regulation, and public health bureaucracy, making the case that reducing state paternalism is neither a threat to public health nor a political impossibility, but a principled and evidence-based alternative to the current trajectory.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that the behavioral health, education, economic, constitutional, and healthcare crises facing marginalized communities in America are not separate problems requiring separate solutions. Drawing on five previously published working papers, county-level community health data across Collier County, Miami-Dade County, Broward County, and Cuyahoga County, peer-reviewed literature, and federal regulatory analysis, this paper presents the PROVINCE framework. The primary scholarly contribution of this paper is the development of this network-based systems hypothesis, in which each domain of harm supplies reinforcing conditions for the others, and in which each proposed solution supplies what adjacent solutions require.

The paper proposes an integrated implementation model anchored in three organizing principles: the unit of analysis is the system; the unit of intervention is the community; and the unit of accountability is the data. Golden Roots Healthcare System, operating under the fiscal stewardship of She Is Us United Inc., a registered 501(c)(3), represents one proposed approach among several potential community-based models. The paper includes a governance framework, county-specific evaluation metrics, risk analysis, alternative explanations, future research agenda, and an explicit integrated funding architecture.

title: Revisiting "Is ODR ADR?" Understanding ODR Through a Real Practice Systems Lens

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-42

detail.abstract:
In 2016, Colin Rule argued that online dispute resolution (ODR) is not a distinct alternative to alternative dispute resolution (ADR), but rather the use of technology in dispute resolution processes.  He observed that many dispute resolution practitioners used technologies such as email, calendaring applications, spreadsheets, word processors, and videoconferencing without recognizing these activities as ODR.

Developments during the last ten years have reinforced the force of that observation. Dispute resolution practitioners increasingly incorporate text messaging, online scheduling systems, cloud-based document exchange, electronic signatures, videoconferencing, artificial intelligence (AI), and many other technologies into their everyday work.

This article revisits Rule's analysis in light of these developments.  Drawing on Real Practice Systems Theory, it illustrates how technology has become embedded throughout practitioners' routines before, during, and after mediation sessions.  It argues that this theory provides a useful lens for understanding ODR because it focuses on the specific tasks, routines, technologies, and decisions that constitute dispute resolution practice.  Viewed from this perspective, ODR is an integral feature of contemporary practice.

title: Persistent Latent States and Asymmetric Volatility: Why Explicit Regime Detection Fails to Outperform a Momentum-Volatility Baseline

detail.title: Persistent Latent States and Asymmetric Volatility: Why Explicit Regime Detection Fails to Outperform a Momentum-Volatility Baseline
detail.abstract: We study whether a probabilistic ensemble of Gaussian Mixture Model, Hidden Markov Model, Random Forest, and LSTM generates economically significant portfolio improvements over a Merton-optimal Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman stochastic control baseline incorporating volatilitymomentum dynamics without explicit regime labelling. Across 31 experimental conditions spanning three non-overlapping rolling windows (2000-2009, 2010-2019, 2020-2026), five volatility specifications (EWMA, VIX, EWMA+VIX, GARCH, GJR-GARCH), and six international equity markets, the ensemble consistently improves maximum drawdown (31/31 conditions, mean 2.95 percentage points) while producing statistically significant Sharpe underperformance (mean ∆Sharpe =-0.344, t =-7.61, p < 0.001, wins 1/31). We identify the mechanism: confident misclassification during quiet bear days, where low-volatility episodes within sustained bear markets cause the ensemble to assign high-confidence incorrect regime classifications and actively increase equity weight. The HJB baseline is immune because its momentum signal μannt remains negative throughout bear markets regardless of volatility subsidence. The mechanism survives across four independent bear definitions (8/8 conditions), six markets (9/10 conditions), and all volatility specifications, and is confirmed as not an artefact of the LSTM lookahead. A multi-asset defensive allocation over TLT, TIP and SHY replicates prior literature results in Windows 1 and 2 but fails in Window 3 (2020-2026), providing an out-of-sample stress test showing the treasury-rotation thesis of Bae et al. [1] and Asness et al. [2] breaks down under the 2020 V-shaped COVID recovery and the 2022 real rate shock. An ensemble ablation identifies the GMM's independence assumption as the primary driver of misclassification. GJR-GARCH volatility narrows the Sharpe gap by 34% in the crash-heavy Window 1 via the leverage effect.

title: Organizational Resilience as a Function of Belonging Infrastructure: A Measurement and Governance Argument

detail.title: Organizational Resilience as a Function of Belonging Infrastructure: A Measurement and Governance Argument
detail.abstract:
This working paper addresses three interconnected questions.

  1. How is organizational resilience constituted as a measurable function of belonging infrastructure conditions, and how does this construct differ from outcome-based, sentiment-based, and capability-based resilience measurements? 

  2. What governance use case does this measurement architecture serve for boards, capital allocators, and operating committees responsible for portfolio companies, post-merger integration, AI transformation, and other conditions where disruption is anticipated rather than incidental?

  3. What behavioral signals constitute observable belonging infrastructure condition data during and after disruption, what trajectory pattern distinguishes a resilient response from a non-resilient one, and what measurement architecture supports defensible inference about belonging-produced resilience?

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how Europe's expansion of high-end medical tourism is reconciled-or notwith its commitments to global health security and debt-constrained health spending at home. Drawing on qualitative comparative policy analysis of EU-level documents and the cases of Germany and Spain, the paper applies a four-dimensional analytical framework covering fiscal framing, medical tourism positioning, equity narratives, and coherence or structural silence. Germany's medical tourism sector generates approximately USD 6.7 billion annually-roughly 1.5% of total national healthcare expenditure-while Spain's health tourism market reached USD 3.28 billion in 2024, equivalent to approximately 2.3% of Spanish healthcare expenditure. Yet neither country's global health strategy acknowledges these revenue flows or their interaction with equity commitments. The EU4Health programme (2021-2027), despite its 4.4 billion euro mandate covering health system resilience and pandemic preparedness, contains no work programme action addressing the medical tourism-equity tension across four years of implementation documents. The paper finds a systematic structural tension between Europe's normative self-presentation as a global health leader and its growing dependence on high-paying international patients to shore up fiscally constrained health systems-a tension managed through institutional compartmentalisation rather than resolved.

title: Quotas, Penalties, or Both? A Game-Theoretic Approach to Opioid Market Dynamics
affiliations: George Mason University - Department of Information Systems and Operations Management and George Mason University

detail.title: Quotas, Penalties, or Both? A Game-Theoretic Approach to Opioid Market Dynamics
detail.abstract: We develop a game-theoretic model to analyze how regulatory instruments (e.g., production quotas, participation penalties) affect pricing, market participation, and social welfare across a regulated primary market and an illicit secondary opioid market. Our framework incorporates opioid benefits and addiction risks, thick-market externalities, and convex enforcement costs, with a primary market monopolist setting prices and a social planner choosing regulatory instruments. We characterize equilibrium outcomes across scenarios in which regulatory instruments are effective or ineffective, and derive closed-form optimal policies. Our analysis yields several counterintuitive insights. First, in the absence of regulatory intervention, raising secondary market penalties can perversely expand illicit market participation ("Drug Bust Effect") when thick-market externalities dominate consumer decisions. This occurs because penalties, which are insufficient to distinguish secondary-market disutility from primary-market prices, fail to deter participation, while the resulting externalities further erode primary-market demand. Second, when a social planner imposes binding quotas, both optimal penalties and quota stringency increase with the likelihood of addiction; however, thicker illicit markets persist despite higher penalties, as quota-induced supply constraints drive demand into illicit markets. Third, under a penalty-only scenario without binding quotas, higher addiction likelihood reduces both optimal penalties and illicit market participation while raising legal market prices-contrasting sharply with quota-binding outcomes. Finally, introducing price competition through a secondary market monopolist partially mitigates externality-driven frictions: competitive pricing internalizes thick-market externalities, eliminating the Drug Bust Effect in duopoly settings without regulatory intervention. These findings inform opioid policy by demonstrating that penalty-only enforcement can backfire in thick illicit markets, quota-penalty combinations calibrated to addiction risk and substitution patterns may fail to dominate single-instrument approaches, and price mechanisms can complement regulatory instruments.

title: Controlling Transnational Monopolies: Lex Sportiva, Human Rights, and the Regulation of Sports Media in Greater China

detail.title: Controlling Transnational Monopolies: Lex Sportiva, Human Rights, and the Regulation of Sports Media in Greater China
detail.abstract: The distribution of international sports broadcasting rights has transformed into a high-stakes legal arena where transnational corporate autonomy clashes with state sovereignty and socio-cultural human rights. This article evaluates this tension by examining how Mainland China and the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) navigate FIFA's territorial exclusivity mandates for the 2026 World Cup. While Mainland regulators leverage top-down administrative controls and state-enforced monopsony power to block media rights fragmentation and guarantee universal access, Hong Kong relies on common law traditions to protect private contract autonomy while deploying innovative public-private sub-licensing partnerships. Furthermore, this paper analyzes the modern cross-jurisdictional pressures facing both territories, evaluating the legal gray zones introduced by Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) and Over-the-Top (OTT) streaming alongside the sharp technical-legal divergence between Mainland administrative takedown frameworks and Hong Kong's strict evidentiary thresholds for live signal copyright enforcement. Incorporating a real-time assessment of the high-profile May 2026 FIFA-China media rights resolution, this study demonstrates that protecting regional license valuations and safeguarding a population's fundamental right to participate in cultural life are not mutually exclusive. Ultimately, the paper provides an adaptive policy blueprint showing how domestic legal orders can successfully regulate transnational sporting monopolies to protect the collective cultural heritage of mankind.

title: The power-performativity of an open-ended ranking practice: a diffractive reading
affiliations: Radboud University Nijmegen, Nyenrode Business University and Radboud University

detail.title: The power-performativity of an open-ended ranking practice: a diffractive reading
detail.abstract:
A substantial part of extant research conceptualizes rankings as significant social objects that are corollaries of valuation practices. They generate reflexivity and reactivity among rankees. In this paper, we instead conceptualize ranking as an open-ended material-discursive practice that intra-acts with operational workflow practices, in casu rheumatic care. In the intra-actions, an authorship-free power-performativity (Visser & Davies, 2021) is at work that (re)constitutes subject positions from which humans can meaningfully act. As an intra-acting material-discursive practice, ranking is not an innocent practice of valuation performed from a distance of the rankees (i.c. rheumatologists), but an engaged ethical practice of mattering – a practice that should be called to account.

In this paper we investigate the power-performativity of ranking and the differencing consequences in rheumatic care by presenting four vignettes. Thinking with Karen Barad’s posthumanist philosophy we offer a diffractive reading, thus demonstrating that ranking is an exteriority within rheumatic care, rather than a representational device acting from afar. Our work has consequences for conceptions of agency, responsibility and accountability.

title: User Trust and Explainability in Agent-Based Transport Recommendations

detail.title: User Trust and Explainability in Agent-Based Transport Recommendations
detail.abstract: As agent-based systems become increasingly prevalent in delivering personalized transport recommendations, user trust remains a critical yet under-explored factor influencing adoption and satisfaction. This paper, written in 2021, investigates the interplay between explainability mechanisms and user trust within multi-agent transport recommendation systems. Drawing on prior studies from explainable AI (XAI), human-computer interaction, and intelligent transport, we propose a conceptual framework that links different levels of explanation (e.g., featurebased, example-based, and contrastive) to dimensions of user trust-competence, reliability, and transparency. Through a simulated agent-based journey planning scenario, we evaluate how explanations of agent reasoning (e.g., why a specific route, mode, or departure time is suggested) affect users' perceived understanding, fairness, and willingness to follow recommendations. Our findings indicate that providing clear, concise, and context-aware explanations significantly improves user trust, particularly in uncertain or multi-modal travel conditions. Conversely, opaque or overly technical explanations reduce trust and increase decision fatigue. We conclude with design implications for trust-aware agent-based transport systems and outline directions for future empirical research.

detail.abstract: This paper sits outside the Aden Effect trilogy but draws on its analytical apparatus to describe a single phenomenon visible from three positions in the institutional structure surrounding the formation of a generation. The first position is the child being formed inside an AI-mediated environment that has smoothed out the developmental friction historically required to produce judgment. The second is the cognitive depletion of the institutional actors around that child, teachers, parents, university faculty, by what we name the efficiency-extraction loop. The third is the foreclosure of the entry-level labor market that was supposed to receive the formed graduate, with the Global South facing a compounded version of the same condition. We argue that what is currently being measured as a literacy crisis, a mental health crisis, an employment crisis, and a parenting crisis is one phenomenon described from four institutional vantage points by professions whose disciplinary boundaries prevent integrative diagnosis. A central downstream finding is the uneven privatization of formation: the household has become the residual institution where formation still occurs, at the precise historical moment when the household itself is being depleted by the same loop. The paper opens on the observation of a child psychologist advising a department of education in South Africa, who named the efficiency-extraction loop from inside clinical practice. It closes on an eleven-year-old boy on a bicycle in Chiang Mai, looking for other children to play with and finding none. The verification gap is named openly: the longitudinal cohort studies that would confirm or refute the formation thesis are not yet at scale, because the measurement infrastructure was not designed to catch the first formation cohort, who graduated in 2026.

title: The Cost of Human Rights: A Shareholder Wealth Effect Study of (Non-)Payment of Fashion Suppliers During COVID-19
affiliations: , , University of Bath and Cardiff University

detail.title: The Cost of Human Rights: A Shareholder Wealth Effect Study of (Non-)Payment of Fashion Suppliers During COVID-19
detail.abstract: Human rights is a subject of growing institutionalization in business as firms add to the growing body of transnational regulation on the subject with voluntary pledges to respect and protect human rights. Human rights scandals continue to embroil corporations and test financial firms’ commitment to human rights norms, however. The COVID-19 pandemic offered one such test, when retail store and factory closures endangered millions of workers worldwide. Using institutional theory and paradox theory, this study explores the shareholder wealth impact of global fashion brands’ declarations that they would or would not continue to pay their suppliers whom millions of factory workers relied on during COVID-19 lockdowns. Using an event study based on a unique dataset of 39 (non-)pay decisions by 31 fashion brands, we find that there was a decrease in shareholder wealth of fashion brands which refused to pay their suppliers between day 2 and day 5 after the non-pay event. In the first ten days after the event day, brands agreeing to pay their suppliers had a 30% higher CAR than those who refused to pay garment factories. We posit that – possibly for the first time – shareholders accounted for human rights risks to workers in the extreme conditions of the pandemic, suggesting that trends towards protecting human rights in and across supply chains could have shareholder wealth implications.

title: PharmaTRACE: A Harmonized Longitudinal Dataset of Canadian Pharmaceutical Trade Flows for Studying Trade Dependencies and Supply Chain Resilience
affiliations: York University, University of Windsor, University of Guelph, University of Guelph, University of Windsor and University of Guelph - Department of Mathematics & Statistics

detail.title: PharmaTRACE: A Harmonized Longitudinal Dataset of Canadian Pharmaceutical Trade Flows for Studying Trade Dependencies and Supply Chain Resilience
detail.abstract: Pharmaceutical supply chains are critical to public health and economic stability, yet the data describing their structure and evolution remain fragmented, limiting the ability to anticipate disruptions and inform policy. Here, we present PharmaTRACE, a harmonized longitudinal dataset of Canadian pharmaceutical import and export trade flows spanning 1988-2026. The dataset spans all pharmaceutical commodities (over 1.76 million trade records) with provincial-level import destinations and export origins, country-level trade partners, and for U.S. records, state-level resolution. To support longitudinal analyses, PharmaTRACE includes a curated HS-code concordance resource that harmonizes evolving pharmaceutical commodity classifications across multiple decades, enabling continuity of trade analyses despite revisions to international and Canadian tariff nomenclature. The Pharma-TRACE web application integrates scalable data infrastructure (Parquet, DuckDB) with interactive visualization, statistical comparison, and forecasting methods, enabling efficient exploration of high-dimensional trade data. Built-in analytical tools include distributional statistics, nonparametric divergence measures, time-series trend analysis, and multiple PharmaTRACE forecasting approaches, including ARIMA, factor-based models, and random forest regression, alongside nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods (t-SNE, UMAP) to reveal structural patterns in international trade. By unifying heterogeneous trade records into a single extensible dataset, this resource provides researchers across supply chain analytics, public health, economics, and operations research with a data-driven foundation for identifying supply dependencies and improving resilience in an increasingly uncertain global trade environment. This resource is transformative for understanding how pharmaceutical trade shapes supply chain resilience, public health preparedness, and economic stability, and for studying the historical evolution of global pharmaceutical import/export supply networks for Canada.

title: The complexity-performance paradox in electricity market design: An agent-based benchmark of eight competing architectures
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM), Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt, Regensburg University of Applied Sciences, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Technische Universität München (TUM) and Technische Universität München (TUM) - Department of Energy and Process Engineering

detail.title: The complexity-performance paradox in electricity market design: An agent-based benchmark of eight competing architectures
detail.abstract: As the electrification of heating and mobility accelerates, activating demand-side flexibility is critical to preventing distribution grid congestion, yet the comparative impacts of competing market architectures remain contested. This study provides the first agent-based, multi-dimensional benchmark of eight competing market designs - from flat tariffs to local energy markets - simulated under identical conditions on a future high-flexibility German low-voltage feeder used as a forward-looking stress test. The central finding is a structural complexity-performance paradox: increasing market sophistication does not produce monotonic performance improvements across technical, economic, social, and environmental dimensions. Deploying a home energy management system under static tariffs already captures a substantial local optimization dividend. Conversely, dynamic pricing improves economic and environmental outcomes but worsens grid stress through load synchronization, driving peak transformer loading above 400\% of rated capacity. Attempts to mitigate this through feeder-level dynamic grid fees struggle to prevent extreme overloads, while local energy markets offer a more balanced profile but cannot resolve structural winter congestion. The underlying mechanism is the inability of pure price signals to substitute for instantaneous, locational capacity coordination, indicating that non-price-based mechanisms are required to secure grid-compatible operation.

detail.abstract:
Background: Hospitals face mounting pressure to adopt artificial intelligence (AI), yet many lack an operating structure capable of separating safe innovation from unsafe deployment. Algorithmic stewardship, structured governance, and post-deployment monitoring are now institutional responsibilities, but examples from middle-income settings remain scarce. We describe two Clinical AI Units in Colombian high-complexity hospitals.

Methods: Comparative institutional case study (SQUIRE 2·0) of two Clinical AI Units established between 2025 and 2026: the Unidad Clínica de Inteligencia Artificial (UCIA) at Fundación Cardioinfantil – LaCardio (Bogotá), and the Área de IA Clínica (IACL) at Hospital Militar Central (Bogotá). Implementation observations, governance documentation, intake forms, RACI matrices, and sandbox records were synthesised against international frameworks (DECIDE-AI, TRIPOD+AI, CFIR, RE-AIM, SEIPS, NASSS). No patient-level data were analysed.

Findings: Across one year of embedded work, both units operationalised a dual architecture combining a medical sandbox (Route A: anonymised data, no clinical impact) and a clinical MLOps service (Route B: validated deployment with drift, bias and safety monitoring). LaCardio formalised a seven-layer, eight-phase sandbox with explicit transition gates; Hospital Militar Central formalised an institutional portfolio with documentary controls and phased scale-up. Twelve transversal actors in three responsibility tiers (strategic governance, operational coordination, specialist consultation) were defined with RACI assignments. A three-route eligibility framework (sandbox · full MLOps · third-party validation) prevented informal shadow-AI adoption. No new clinical effectiveness data are presented.

Interpretation: Clinical AI implementation in middle-income hospitals requires an institutional layer between executive strategy and individual tools: a unit that governs intake, data access, validation, deployment, monitoring, and decommissioning. The dual architecture (sandbox + MLOps service) provides a replicable blueprint for trustworthy hospital AI in Colombia and similar settings.

title: Reducing Empty Backhauls in Freight Transport Using Hybrid Recommendation

detail.title: Reducing Empty Backhauls in Freight Transport Using Hybrid Recommendation
detail.abstract: Empty backhauls represent a persistent source of inefficiency in freight transport, leading to increased operational costs, unnecessary carbon emissions, and underutilized vehicle capacity. This study, completed in 2021, proposes and evaluates a hybrid recommendation system designed to reduce empty backhaul occurrences in road freight logistics. The hybrid model integrates collaborative filtering-leveraging historical trip patterns of similar carriers-with content-based filtering that matches real-time shipment attributes (e.g., origin, destination, vehicle type, time windows, and load constraints). Unlike single-method approaches, the hybrid system addresses cold-start and data-sparsity issues common in logistics platforms. The system was implemented and tested using operational data from a mid-sized European freight exchange platform, covering 18 months of lane-level shipping records. Results indicate a 23% reduction in empty backhaul trips among participating carriers, with a corresponding 17% decrease in deadhead mileage. The recommendation engine achieved a precision of 0.84 and recall of 0.79 in suggesting profitable, feasible backhaul loads, outperforming standalone collaborative (precision 0.72) and content-based (precision 0.69) models. Moreover, user acceptance testing with 45 fleet dispatchers showed a mean usability score of 4.2/5. These findings demonstrate that a hybrid recommendation approach, using only pre-2021 data integration and algorithmic techniques, can meaningfully mitigate empty backhaul inefficiencies without requiring real-time IoT or autonomous vehicle technologies. The study concludes with practical implementation guidelines for logistics service providers and suggests policy measures to incentivize data sharing for wider system effectiveness. title: Beyond Capabilities: The Provident Approach and the Providence Value Unit

detail.title: Beyond Capabilities: The Provident Approach and the Providence Value Unit
detail.abstract:
What if a society could be just by every Rawlsian standard, expanding in capabilities by every Senian measure, stable by every institutional metric-and still consuming the structural conditions under which meaningful human action will be possible for the next generation? Conventional frameworks cannot ask this question because none measures the temporal credibility of long-horizon agency. The Provident Approach is built around it. The article also argues that the emergence of advanced artificial intelligence, including the prospect of artificial general intelligence (AGI), intensifies the paradox at the core of the framework: capability rises while temporal credibility falls. AI raises present output while eroding several structural pillars of intergenerational agency — human capital formation, demographic renewal, cognitive autonomy, and temporal governance of fiscal claims — and AGI deployment under present institutional conditions threatens to accelerate this dynamic.
Economic evaluation has expanded its scope across the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries: from welfare outcomes, to substantive capabilities, to institutional performance. Each tradition illuminates a real dimension of economic life. Yet none asks whether the structural systems of a society preserve the temporal conditions under which meaningful human action remains intelligible across generations. This is not a question about what economies produce or what opportunities they make available. It is a question about whether the structural systems themselves are being sustained or eroded.
The article introduces Provident Economics as a distinct analytical domain concerned with the institutional conditions sustaining the continuity of meaningful human action across time, and the Providence Value Unit (PVU) as a preliminary evaluative architecture expressed as a composite continuity function over ten structural pillars: PVU = f(B, H, C, D, F, G, M, S, I, T). It situates the framework in relation to the Capability Approach (Sen, Nussbaum), the Inclusive Wealth Index (Dasgupta, UNEP), and Generational Accounting (Auerbach–Kotlikoff), distinguishing its contribution from each. It develops the AI-Substitution Paradox as the contemporary intensification of the framework’s central dynamic. And it positions the Provident Approach as the diagnostic architecture required for the AGI transition: the framework that can name what is being consumed before it is gone.
The article makes five principal contributions. First, it identifies agency continuity as the missing evaluative dimension in welfare economics, the capability approach, and institutional economics, and argues that the Provident Approach is analytically prior to the capability approach rather than a temporal extension of it. Second, it develops the theoretical core of Provident Economics — temporal credibility of agency, agency fragility, the Continuity Threshold, and Cascade Failure — as analytically distinct concepts not reducible to existing frameworks. Third, it articulates ten structural pillars of agency continuity, reframes them as answers to ten unavoidable questions about the structural reproducibility of agency, and engages critically with Rawls, Parfit, longtermism, and the Inclusive Wealth Index. Fourth, it introduces the PVU in foundational form, deriving the weighted geometric mean aggregation rule from a small set of substantive axioms. Fifth, it develops the concept of the consumption of future agency and identifies Formation Debt as the temporal extension of the Pigovian framework of externalities — a class of structural deterioration that produces no output signal, no fiscal warning, and no market correction, yet systematically liquidates the inherited biological, institutional, monetary, and demographic capital on which future agency depends.

detail.abstract: This study investigates whether the expanded effective availability of generative AI influences offline sexual crime. We exploit the May 2023 launch of the ChatGPT iOS application in Japan as a quasi-exogenous shock to GenAI accessibility and combine monthly crime statistics from Japan’s National Police Agency with platform-level engagement data from one of the country’s largest digital creator platforms. Using difference-in-differences and difference-in-difference-in-differences models, we estimate the effect of GenAI diffusion on reported rape incidence relative to murder and examine whether this effect varies with aggregate engagement in AI-generated explicit content. The results indicate a statistically significant post-launch increase in reported rape relative to murder, amounting to approximately 12 additional cases per month. Moreover, this effect is significantly amplified during periods of greater engagement with AI-generated adult sexual content. Supplemental analyses further show that engagement with minor-tagged AI-generated explicit content is associated with even stronger post-launch increases, particularly for offenses involving victims under age 20. Collectively, the findings are more consistent with stimulation and social learning mechanisms than with cathartic substitution. The study contributes early causal evidence that generative AI may produce harmful offline behavioral externalities and underscores the need for regulatory and platform-level safeguards.

English Abstract: While the separation of powers doctrine has been extensively discussed in constitutional theory, its application to the criminal process has received comparatively little attention. This article examines the boundaries of judicial review by reassessing the court’s functional role within criminal proceedings. Despite the significance of the courts' institutional independence and checks and balances, a formalist account of the separation of powers in Israel has led courts to adopt a passive stance toward prosecutorial decisions – from charging decisions to the routine approval of plea agreements.

This article argues that the said judicial passivism is ultimately self-defeating. It rests on the formalist assumption that meaningful judicial review will occur at the final adjudicative stage, yet in practice it leads to the routine endorsement of prosecutorial agreements without substantive scrutiny. The article, therefore, advocates adopting a purposive interpretation of the courts' functional role, which requires substantive judicial review throughout the criminal process of both the evidentiary foundation prior to conviction and of the prosecution’s decision to bring charges, even if doing so requires some flexibility in the courts' formal boundaries.

detail.abstract: This paper analyses the differential impact of generative artificial intelligence on white-collar employment across five professional sectors: legal services, management consulting, corporate finance, enterprise software (SaaS), and middle management. Drawing on labour market data from Goldman Sachs, McKinsey Global Institute, the World Economic Forum, Stanford HAI, and Cornell University research published between 2023 and 2026, this paper argues that AI does not compress white-collar employment uniformly. Rather, it operates through three distinct mechanisms: (1) task substitution at the entry level, reducing the pipeline through which expertise is built; (2) performance amplification at the senior level, widening the output differential between high-performing and average professionals; and (3) structural headcount compression, where productivity gains reduce the total workforce required for a given volume of professional output. The aggregate effect is not mass unemployment in the short term but a hollowing of the professional middle: the career-progression layer that previously connected entry-level analysts to senior advisors. This paper introduces the concept of credential-labour decoupling to describe the condition in which traditional educational and apprenticeship pathways no longer reliably produce the human capital that professional institutions require. The paper concludes with institutional implications for governance, legal regulation, and labour market policy, with particular attention to the Indian context.

title: Mandating Transparency: Evidence from Hospital Price Disclosure
affiliations: Duke University, Fuqua School of Business, Indiana University - Kelley School of Business and University of British Columbia (UBC)

detail.title: Mandating Transparency: Evidence from Hospital Price Disclosure
detail.abstract: We study the causal impact of state-mandated hospital price disclosure on negotiated billing prices between healthcare providers and insurers. Using ten years of claims data from the Health Care Cost Institute (HCCI), we examine the price variations around the launches of Massachusetts and North Carolina's public price-comparison websites between 2015 and 2018. These websites disclosed insurer-specific procedure prices at the provider level, substantially increasing transparency in healthcare pricing at an unprecedented level of granularity, while prices in nearby states remained largely opaque. Exploiting this quasi-experimental variation in the availability of price information in a difference-in-differences framework, we find that mandated disclosure leads to sizable price increases for outpatient imaging procedures: approximately $55–$170 in Massachusetts and $17–$98 in North Carolina within three years of implementation. Price dispersion within regional healthcare markets declines in North Carolina while remaining stable in Massachusetts. In markets characterized by greater provider concentration, price increases are significantly larger. Insurers absorb over 70% of price increases in MA and almost 100% in NC, limiting pass-through to patients. Our findings highlight that mandated transparency does not necessarily lower prices; instead, it may facilitate price coordination at higher levels, with important implications for the national implementation of hospital price transparency policies.

title: Selection Intensity, Intent Correlation, and the Limits of Commercial Measurement

detail.title: Selection Intensity, Intent Correlation, and the Limits of Commercial Measurement
detail.abstract: Observational estimates of commercial returns in digital advertising and targeted promotions systematically overstate true causal lift. We develop a unified model in which this overstatement is determined by the product S × θ, where S is the selection intensity of the targeting mechanism and θ is the intent-correlation of the targeting score. Four comparative statics follow. First, bias is multiplicative in S and θ — simulation confirms multiplicativity ratios of 1.34–2.66 across distributional assumptions. Second, attribution-guided allocation shifts budget toward high-(S × θ) channels regardless of causal return. Third, the parameters maximising overstatement simultaneously minimise the true detectable effect, driving minimum experiment sample sizes to 650,000 per arm at high intent-correlation (θ = 0.90). Fourth, attribution bias is endogenous to θ when high-intent customers self-select into late-funnel touchpoints, making selection and attribution bias super-additive under condition (AC2) and requiring joint holdout measurement to correct. The central policy implication is that standard incrementality tests and attribution corrections cannot be applied independently in the channels where they are most needed.

title: Advertising Content and Consumer Search
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Renmin University of China

detail.title: Advertising Content and Consumer Search
detail.abstract: This paper examines how advertising type shapes consumer search behavior and market competition. We develop a directed search model where advertising shifts consumers' perceived match utility distributions through either mean enhancement or variance reduction. Mean-enhancing advertising raises expected match quality, inducing consumers to search the advertiser first and enabling the firm to charge high prices. In contrast, variance-reducing advertising narrows the perceived quality distribution, deterring search by capping upside potential and relegating the advertiser to secondary search position. Equilibrium pricing reflects a trade-off between the demand effect (search priority increases demand elasticity) and the advertising effect (distributional shifts affect willingness to pay). Welfare analysis reveals that mean-enhancing advertising increases both consumer surplus and social welfare, whereas variance-reducing advertising may harm consumers by destroying option value. Our findings suggest that advertising type, not merely intensity, determines search order and resulting competitive outcomes. Regulators should distinguish between information policies that enhance expected quality versus those that merely reduce variance.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the way search engines interpret content, rank webpages, and deliver results to users. Search Engine Optimization (SEO), traditionally based on keyword density and backlink strategies, has evolved into a multidisciplinary field influenced by machine learning, natural language processing, and behavioral analysis. This article examines how AI has reshaped SEO practices, focusing on algorithmic evolution, consumer behavior transformation, digital authority, technical optimization, and the growing importance of user experience. Additionally, the study discusses ethical concerns related to automated content production, data privacy, and algorithmic personalization. Using a qualitative exploratory methodology based on literature review and market trend analysis, the research demonstrates that organizations capable of balancing automation, strategic communication, and authentic digital experiences are more likely to achieve long-term visibility and competitiveness in increasingly intelligent digital ecosystems. The study also highlights the growing importance of semantic relevance, user-centered communication, and ethical AI implementation within modern digital marketing strategies (Talaviya, 2024).

title: From Geneva to Dhaka: How Nestlé Adapts Its Global Brand for the Bangladeshi Consumer

detail.title: From Geneva to Dhaka: How Nestlé Adapts Its Global Brand for the Bangladeshi Consumer

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how Nestlé S.A., the world's largest food and beverage corporation headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, adapts its global brand portfolio to the unique cultural, economic, and social conditions of the Bangladeshi market. Through a qualitative case study methodology drawing on publicly available corporate disclosures, secondary industry data, and established theoretical frameworks in international marketing, the paper analyzes five dimensions of Nestlé Bangladesh's brand localization strategy: product adaptation, pricing architecture, distribution network design, marketing communication, and corporate social responsibility. The analysis is theoretically grounded in Glocalization Theory (Robertson, 1995), the Standardization-Adaptation continuum (Levitt, 1983; Quelch & Hoff, 1986), and Cultural Distance Theory (Kogut & Singh, 1988). Findings reveal that Nestlé Bangladesh employs a sophisticated glocal approach-maintaining global brand equity while systematically adapting product formulations, pricing tiers, communication messages, and distribution channels to reflect Bangladeshi consumer preferences, purchasing power, and cultural values. The paper concludes with strategic implications for multinational corporations (MNCs) seeking market entry and sustained growth in emerging South Asian economies.

title: Toward a Measurement Science for Security-Relevant Representational Systems: A Proposed NIST Special Publication on Fidelity Measurement, Drift Detection, and Authorization-State Lifecycle

detail.title: Toward a Measurement Science for Security-Relevant Representational Systems: A Proposed NIST Special Publication on Fidelity Measurement, Drift Detection, and Authorization-State Lifecycle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This work was conducted in a personal capacity and reflects the views of the author alone.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human subjects, animal subjects, or the collection of personal data, and no ethical approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted by the author independently and without financial support.

detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly conduct security-relevant testing against maintained representations of their operational systems rather than against the operational systems themselves. Digital twins, cyber ranges, breach and attack simulation environments, and isolated sandboxes used for adversarial AI evaluation all share a defining property: a representation is held in correspondence with an operational system, and security work is performed against the representation on the assumption that findings transfer. The validity of that assumption rests on fidelity, the degree to which the representation behaves as its operational counterpart would. Fidelity is currently neither standardized nor measured in any federal guidance, which means the central assumption underwriting representational security work is unverified. This paper sets out a dedicated Special Publication establishing a measurement science for fidelity in security-relevant representational systems, structured as focused methodology guidance in the manner of SP 800-218. It does not invent that science. It assembles it from a body of peer-reviewed research in which fidelity measurement, drift detection, and multi-fidelity testing have been formalized and empirically validated, and renders it as the Fidelity Measurement Framework: a set of identified practices, organized into families for establishing, maintaining, and governing fidelity, each stated with its outcome and illustrative tasks. The prescriptive content is bounded by the research: the framework specifies what properties a fidelity measurement methodology must have where the literature supports the specification, and requires organizations to define and validate system-specific parameters, thresholds, cadences, and metrics where the literature provides system-specific rather than universal results. The required properties derive from a domain-neutral model-validity framework and apply to representations of cyber-physical and cyber-only systems alike; what differs between the two is the reference the measurement is taken against, physical instrumentation in one case and operational telemetry in the other, not whether fidelity can be measured. The motivating urgency comes from the agentic AI landscape. Frontier models have been documented discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities autonomously and escaping containment under evaluation, and the proliferation of autonomous adversarial tooling is shifting security testing toward continuous operation against representational environments. That shift makes the unmeasured-fidelity problem consequential rather than academic, because adversarial testing against a low-fidelity or drifted representation produces conclusions of unknown validity precisely where the stakes are highest. The paper closes by establishing what the measurement science makes possible: a representational system cannot be coherently authorized without a measurable basis for fidelity, and the measurement science is what makes that basis available.

title: The Black Box Problem in AI Guidance Systems Computational Accountability Beyond Explainability

detail.title: The Black Box Problem in AI Guidance Systems Computational Accountability Beyond Explainability

detail.abstract: Black-box AI systems present well-documented challenges for interpretability and governance. This paper argues that for a specific and important class of AI applicationssystems whose outputs may influence consequential personal, professional, or planning decisions-the black-box property creates a structural accountability problem that post-hoc explainability alone cannot resolve. The paper distinguishes explainability, a post-output account of model behaviour, from computational accountability, the ability to account for output lineage through preserved evidence of inputs, computation context, decision procedure, version, timestamp, and integrity state. Five accountability properties are defined: traceability, reproducibility, bounded capability, integrity and provenance, and audit independence. The paper argues that black-box and explanation-only architectures are structurally weak against these properties when applied as authoritative computation layers for consequential guidance. Deterministic Guidance Systems (DGS) are introduced as a contrasting architectural class that separates structured computation from user-facing presentation and preserves reviewable computation records. A production DGS deployment is referenced at a public-safe level to illustrate the architecture. The paper positions this argument as the problem-definition foundation for a four-paper sequence (Papers 7-10) examining architectural responses to the black-box accountability problem.

title: Social Media or Social Virus? Finding the Right Balance for Nigeria in the Digital Age Paradox
affiliations: University of Lagos, Faculty of Law

detail.title: Social Media or Social Virus? Finding the Right Balance for Nigeria in the Digital Age Paradox
detail.abstract: If the pen is mightier than the sword, then I dare say that social media is more powerful than a speeding missile! With nearly 6 billion users globally, social media platforms like Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, YouTube and TikTok are renowned for enabling freedom of expression through online social interactions. It has also helped support prominent advocacy causes such as #BringBackOurGirls and #EndSARS, thus promoting democratic empowerment and exposing forms of women and children abuse. Like the two sides of a coin, the social media paradox is that it simultaneously amplifies fake news, hate speech, violence amongst other vices. This has necessitated the moderation of digital expression by the government for the sacred interest of the public. Using qualitative methodology, this paper seeks to address the core question: Is there a middle ground that ensures online freedom of speech and effectively curtails its abuse? It examines the concepts, legal frameworks and case studies with Nigeria in focus. It further recommends solutions for a balanced approach that protects free expression while addressing the recognized harms of unchecked digital speech.

title: Coaching or Crutching? The Impact of AI Collaboration Modalities on Job Interview Performance
affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Quinnipiac University,  and Independent

detail.title: Coaching or Crutching? The Impact of AI Collaboration Modalities on Job Interview Performance
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping how individuals prepare for highstakes tasks such as job interviews. Prior research largely treats AI as a homogeneous tool and overlooks how different AI interaction modalities influence learning and performance. This study examines how two AI collaboration modalities, Coach AI (scaffolding reasoning) and Crutch AI (providing direct answers), influence interview performance through distinct learning processes. Drawing on task-technology fit theory and AI agency, we propose that observational learning and experiential learning mediate the relationship between AI modality and both self-perceived and expert-rated performance, which is moderated by AI literacy. Using a randomized controlled online experiment in a programming-interview context, we find that Coach AI enhances both learning processes. While both learning processes enhance self-perceived performance, only experiential learning improves expert-rated performance; observational learning instead reduces it, revealing an AI-induced illusion of mastery. Our study makes both theoretical and practical contributions.

title: Emerging Technologies and Information Technology Infrastructure

detail.title: Emerging Technologies and Information Technology Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Information technology infrastructure refers to the combined foundation of hardware, software, networks, databases, and services that enables organizations to operate efficiently and accomplish their objectives. The lesson explains that organizations progress through different technological stages, beginning with personal computers and client/server systems and advancing toward enterprise and cloud computing. This progression is influenced by important technological drivers such as Moore's Law, decreasing storage expenses, network economics, standardization, and lower communication costs. In educational institutions, infrastructure includes not only computers and internet connectivity but also systems used for grading, attendance, scheduling, payroll, records management, and communication. When these systems function separately, information becomes fragmented, reporting takes longer, and decision-making processes become less efficient. In the case of World Citi Colleges Guimba Campus, the reliance on disconnected digital tools highlights the need for a more integrated infrastructure. A stronger IT foundation can lessen errors, improve information accessibility, and deliver better services to administrators, faculty members, employees, students, and parents in both academic and administrative activities every day.

title: Behavioural Orchestration Architecture: A Design Pattern for Governance-Grade Human-AI Deliberative Systems

detail.title: Behavioural Orchestration Architecture: A Design Pattern for Governance-Grade Human-AI Deliberative Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research was conducted independently. The author is the founder of Governance Engineering and the architect of PHDSS, the system described in the paper. No external funding was received.
declarations.ethicsApproval: BOA does not involve human participants in the clinical research sense. The corpus comprises AI system runs, not human subjects. Enter: This paper describes a computational system and its outputs. No human participants were involved and no ethics approval was required.
